title: Assessing the effect of error field penetration during plasma current ramp-up in the DIII-D tokamak
summary: This work provides evidence that established error field penetration threshold scalings remain applicable during plasma current ramp-up. In dedicated DIII-D experiments with imposed $n=1$ perturbations during extended $I_p$ ramps, an apparent empirical threshold is found between $2$ and $3$~kA of applied 3D coil current, above which MHD modes are seeded. The imposed perturbation couples to the rational surfaces present during the ramp, seeding near the $q=4$ surface and penetrating as an $m/n=3/1$ mode by the end of the perturbation phase. To interpret these observations, multi-machine penetration threshold scalings are combined with equilibrium-based overlap metrics from the GPEC code, including the in-situ error fields of the device. This modeling reproduces the observed onset in the amplitude scan and classifies mode seeding across a database of 12 ramp-up discharges spanning a range of plasma currents and densities. Across this database, the seeding appears to be controlled primarily by the applied 3D coil current rather than by the plasma current or its ramp rate. Accounting for the in-situ error fields is found to be important for reliable prediction. These results are consistent with the robustness of scaling-based penetration metrics when coupled to detailed 3D field modeling under transient ramp-up conditions, and suggest the importance of accounting for in-situ error fields when assessing additional externally induced perturbations. This work is motivated by future tokamaks in which transient, non-axisymmetric error fields can arise during startup, for example from runaway electron mitigation coils.

AI.tldr: This work shows that established error field penetration threshold scalings remain valid during plasma current ramp-up in DIII-D tokamak experiments. They find an empirical threshold between 2-3 kA of applied 3D coil current that seeds MHD modes (penetrating as 3/1 mode near the q=4 surface). Combined GPEC modeling with multi-machine scalings accurately reproduces mode seeding across 12 ramp-up discharges, showing that applied 3D coil current (not plasma current or ramp rate) controls seeding, and that accounting for in-situ error fields is crucial for reliable prediction.
AI.motivation: Future tokamaks (e.g., ITER) may generate transient non-axisymmetric error fields during startup from runaway electron mitigation coils, so it is critical to understand whether existing penetration threshold scalings (developed for steady-state conditions) remain valid under transient ramp-up conditions, and to assess the risk of error field penetration and MHD mode seeding during plasma current ramps.
AI.method: Dedicated DIII-D experiments with imposed n=1 perturbations during extended Ip ramps with amplitude scans; combined multi-machine penetration threshold scalings with equilibrium-based overlap metrics from the GPEC code, including in-situ device error fields, and compared modeling predictions against a database of 12 ramp-up discharges spanning varied plasma currents and densities.
AI.result: An empirical threshold between 2-3 kA of applied 3D coil current seeds MHD modes, penetrating as an m/n=3/1 mode near the q=4 surface. The modeling reproduces the observed onset and classifies mode seeding across the 12-discharge database. Seeding is controlled primarily by applied 3D coil current rather than plasma current or ramp rate, and including in-situ error fields is essential for reliable prediction.
AI.conclusion: Established error field penetration threshold scalings remain robust when coupled with detailed 3D field modeling under transient ramp-up conditions, but accurate prediction requires accounting for in-situ error fields. This has important implications for assessing additional externally induced perturbations (e.g., from runaway electron mitigation coils) in future tokamaks during startup.

title: Activated carbon-assisted anionic dye decomposition using a dual-liquid post-double dielectric barrier discharge plasma reactor
summary: Non-thermal Plasma (NTP) technology, including the Dielectric Barrier Discharge (DBD) reactor, has emerged as an effective advanced oxidation process (AOP) for treating persistent organic pollutants in industrial wastewater. Based on this objective, a dual-liquid dielectric-barrier-discharge plasma reactor was built and used to degrade a ternary anionic dye mixture comprising Reactive Red 120, Congo Red, and Methyl Orange in its post-discharge configuration. The adjustable length of the outer liquid electrode (grounded) provides flexibility in controlling the discharge length and cooling, thereby achieving higher degradation efficiency and greater reactor stability. The conducting-liquid high-voltage electrode (a dielectric tube filled with a conductive solution) helps mitigate metal corrosion and oxidation caused by reactive species in the discharge zone. A detailed study of the degradation of ternary anionic dye mixtures (simulated dye wastewater samples) in the presence of activated carbon (AC) was performed to explore the potential applications of post-discharge treatment. The activated carbon (granules) enhances the degradation rate of ternary anionic dye mixtures in basic solutions rather than in acidic or neutral solutions. A comparative study of the degradation reaction kinetics of the ternary anionic dye mixtures in acidic and basic solutions was conducted after analyzing UV-Vis absorption spectra. The role of other parameters, such as solution pH, the mass and size of AC particles, dye concentrations, and AC reuse, was investigated in relation to degradation efficiency. The degradation mechanism was elucidated by the formation of strong oxidizer (hydroxyl radicals) on the surface of activated carbon during post-discharge treatment. However, in acidic or neutral anionic dye solutions, the degradation mechanism was dominated by ozone.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a dual-liquid dielectric-barrier-discharge (DBD) plasma reactor for degrading a ternary anionic dye mixture (Reactive Red 120, Congo Red, Methyl Orange) in post-discharge configuration, combined with activated carbon (AC) granules to enhance degradation efficiency. The system performs better in basic solutions via hydroxyl radical formation on AC surfaces, while ozone dominates degradation in acidic/neutral conditions.
AI.motivation: Non-thermal plasma technology is a promising advanced oxidation process for treating persistent organic pollutants in industrial wastewater, but reactor designs face challenges including metal corrosion, oxidation from reactive species, and limited degradation efficiency—motivating the development of a more stable and tunable reactor configuration.
AI.method: A dual-liquid DBD plasma reactor was built with an adjustable outer liquid electrode (grounded) to control discharge length and cooling, and a conducting-liquid high-voltage electrode to prevent corrosion. Post-discharge degradation of ternary anionic dye mixtures was studied with activated carbon granules, examining parameters such as pH, AC mass/size, dye concentration, and AC reuse, supported by UV-Vis spectral analysis and kinetics studies.
AI.result: Activated carbon enhanced the degradation rate of ternary anionic dye mixtures in basic solutions more effectively than in acidic or neutral solutions. The mechanism in basic conditions involves hydroxyl radicals generated on AC surfaces, while ozone dominates in acidic/neutral conditions, indicating pH-dependent degradation pathways.
AI.conclusion: The dual-liquid DBD reactor offers flexible discharge control and reduced corrosion issues, and when combined with activated carbon, provides pH-dependent degradation mechanisms—hydroxyl radical-driven in basic media and ozone-driven in acidic/neutral media—for effective treatment of anionic dye wastewater.

title: Revisiting kinetic electrostatic electron non-linear (KEEN) waves in the presence of dynamical ions
comment: This paper was submitted to Springer Proceedings of the 34th International Symposium on Rarefied Gas Dynamics
summary: We revisit the kinetic electrostatic electron nonlinear (KEEN) waves studied by Afeyan et. al in 2014 using a hybrid flow-mapping strategy that combines the characteristic mapping method (CMM) with numerical flow iteration (NuFi). The study extends the classical setup to dynamical ions, comparing their impact on the long-time KEEN dynamics with the static-ion case. To this end, we extend the CMM-NuFI framework with a multi-map strategy, assigning one map to the ion and one to the electron characteristic flow. The resulting problem exhibits a wide separation of spatial and temporal scales, driven by the fine structures generated by the ponderomotive force and by the large ion-to-electron mass ratio, which renders it computationally prohibitive for conventional grid-based methods. Our multi-map CMM-NuFI method efficiently resolves these disparate scales, enabling long-time simulations of KEEN dynamics with fully dynamical ions.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the hybrid CMM-NuFI framework to simulate kinetic electrostatic electron nonlinear (KEEN) waves with dynamical ions using a multi-map strategy, where separate characteristic maps handle ion and electron flows, enabling efficient long-time simulations despite wide spatial and temporal scale separations.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to revisit and extend KEEN wave studies from the static-ion case to fully dynamical ions, which introduces significant computational challenges due to widely separated scales driven by fine ponderomotive structures and the large ion-to-electron mass ratio, making conventional grid-based methods prohibitive.
AI.method: The paper extends the CMM-NuFI framework with a multi-map strategy, assigning one characteristic map to the ion flow and one to the electron flow, enabling efficient resolution of the disparate spatial and temporal scales inherent to the dynamical-ion KEEN wave problem.
AI.result: The multi-map CMM-NuFI method efficiently resolves the disparate scales and enables long-time simulations of KEEN dynamics with fully dynamical ions, comparing their impact on the dynamics against the static-ion case.
AI.conclusion: The multi-map CMM-NuFI approach successfully overcomes the computational hurdles of modeling KEEN waves with dynamical ions, making such long-time simulations tractable and providing new insights into how ion dynamics affect nonlinear kinetic wave behavior.

title: The Erdős similarity conjecture and Rajchman measures
summary: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ support a probability measure whose Fourier--Stieltjes transform tends to zero at infinity. We prove that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there is a closed, $1$-periodic, nowhere dense set $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that \[ m(E\cap I)\ge1-\varepsilon \] for every interval $I$ of length $1$, while $E$ contains no affine copy of $A$. Thus every set supporting a Rajchman measure satisfies the Erdős similarity conjecture in a uniform large-set form. The proof combines equidistribution modulo one for large dilates of the measure with a multiscale family of low-density periodic blockers; no quantitative rate of Fourier decay is used. We also refine a classical theorem of Ivašev-Musatov, showing that for every Hausdorff gauge $h$ there is an $h$-null compact Rajchman support $K$ satisfying \[ \overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}^{\log} K=\dim_{\mathrm P}^{\log} K=1. \] The value $1$ is sharp for both dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that any set supporting a Rajchman measure (i.e., a probability measure whose Fourier-Stieltjes transform vanishes at infinity) can be avoided by a closed, 1-periodic, nowhere dense set E that has measure at least 1-ε in every unit interval. This confirms the Erdős similarity conjecture in a uniform large-set form for Rajchman measure supports. The proof uses equidistribution of large dilates of the measure combined with multiscale periodic blockers. Additionally, the authors refine Ivašev-Musatov's theorem by constructing h-null compact Rajchman supports with logarithmic box-counting and packing dimensions equal to 1, which is sharp.
AI.motivation: The Erdős similarity conjecture asks whether every set of positive measure contains an affine copy of every infinite set. This paper advances understanding by tackling the conjecture through Rajchman measures — a natural class of "thin" sets supporting measures with decaying Fourier coefficients — and aims to establish the conjecture in a stronger uniform large-set sense for this class, while also refining classical dimension results.
AI.method: The proof combines two main ingredients: (1) equidistribution modulo one for large dilates of the Rajchman measure, showing that dilated copies of A spread uniformly; and (2) a multiscale family of low-density periodic blockers used to construct the set E, ensuring it has large measure in every unit interval while avoiding affine copies of A. The construction requires no quantitative rate of Fourier decay, only the qualitative vanishing at infinity. For the dimension refinement, an explicit construction along the lines of Ivašev-Musatov is analyzed via logarithmic gauge dimensions (box-counting and packing).
AI.result: The main theorem shows that for any set A supporting a Rajchman measure and any ε∈(0,1), there exists a closed, 1-periodic, nowhere dense set E with measure at least 1-ε on every unit interval that contains no affine copy of A. This gives a uniform large-set solution to the Erdős similarity conjecture for Rajchman measure supports. Moreover, for every Hausdorff gauge h, there exists an h-null compact Rajchman support K with logarithmic box-counting and packing dimensions equal to 1, improving the classical theorem of Ivašev-Musatov, and the value 1 is shown to be sharp.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that all sets supporting Rajchman measures satisfy the Erdős similarity conjecture in a strong quantitative form (uniform large sets), demonstrating that qualitative Fourier decay alone suffices. The results also provide sharp dimension refinements for Rajchman supports in the logarithmic scaling regime, significantly strengthening classical results.

title: Impact of ion-beam stopping power on proton-boron fusion yield in the pitcher-catcher scheme driven by ultra-intense laser
summary: The effect of stopping power on proton-boron fusion is investigated for a proton beam propagating through boron plasma. Due to the stopping power, the electron temperature of the boron target rises as the proton beam deposits energy. Consequently, a feedback mechanism becomes significant when the trailing part of the beam propagates into the preheated plasma. By coupling this phenomenon with the proton-boron fusion process, fusion yields are systematically investigated by varying the central energy of the proton beam, as well as the thickness and density of the boron target. It is found that, under the influence of stopping power, the optimal central energy for fusion deviates from the intrinsic 672 keV resonance and shifts to approximately 900 keV. Moreover, the present results are substantiated by particle-in-cell simulations, which provides a valuable reference for subsequent high-yield hydrogen-boron fusion.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how stopping power affects proton-boron fusion when a proton beam propagates through boron plasma. The study finds that beam-induced heating of the target creates a feedback mechanism, and the optimal proton beam energy shifts from the intrinsic 672 keV resonance to ~900 keV. Results are validated with particle-in-cell simulations, providing reference for high-yield hydrogen-boron fusion.
AI.motivation: To understand how stopping power—which heats the boron target as the proton beam deposits energy—influences fusion yields, and to identify the optimal beam parameters for proton-boron fusion that have been previously assumed to peak at the intrinsic 672 keV resonance.
AI.method: A systematic parametric study coupling stopping power effects with proton-boron fusion processes, varying the proton beam central energy, boron target thickness, and target density. Results are validated using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations.
AI.result: Under the influence of stopping power, the optimal central proton energy for fusion deviates from the intrinsic 672 keV resonance and shifts to approximately 900 keV.
AI.conclusion: Stopping power plays a significant role in proton-boron fusion by creating a feedback mechanism through target heating, and accounting for it reveals an optimal beam energy (~900 keV) different from the intrinsic resonance. The PIC-validated findings serve as a reference for designing high-yield hydrogen-boron fusion experiments.

title: Linear Growth and Nonlinear Stability of Two-Dimensional MHD Couette Flow with Vertical Dissipation
summary: We study the two-dimensional incompressible magnetohydrodynamic system near the Couette equilibrium $\bigl((y,0)^{\rm T},(β,0)^{\rm T}\bigr)$ on $\mathbb T\times\mathbb R$, in the anisotropic regime where both viscosity and magnetic diffusivity act only in the vertical direction. For the inviscid linearized problem with $|β|>1/2$, we prove sharp linear-in-time growth of the vorticity and current density at the level of the time rate. In contrast, the horizontal components of the velocity and magnetic perturbations remain uniformly bounded, while the vertical components exhibit quantitative inviscid damping at the rate $\langle t\rangle^{-1}$. For the nonlinear problem, we introduce shear-adapted Fourier multipliers that simultaneously capture enhanced dissipation, critical-time effects, and echo-type resonant interactions. Under a suitable horizontal background magnetic field and a quantitative compatibility condition between the magnetic field strength, viscosity, and magnetic diffusivity, we establish global nonlinear stability for divergence-free perturbations satisfying $ \left\| \bigl( \mathbf v_{\rm in}-(y,0)^{\rm T}, \mathbf H_{\rm in}-(β,0)^{\rm T} \bigr) \right\|_{H^N} \leq \varepsilon_0\min\{μ,ν\}^{1/2}, N\geq4$. Moreover, the nonzero horizontal Fourier modes decay in a shear-adapted $H^N$ norm at the enhanced-dissipation rate $e^{-c\min\{μ,ν\}^{1/3}\,t},$ and the vertical velocity and magnetic components gain an additional inviscid-damping factor $\langle t\rangle^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the 2D incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) system near a Couette equilibrium with vertical-only viscosity and magnetic diffusivity. It proves sharp linear-in-time growth of vorticity and current density for the inviscid linearized problem when |β|>1/2, demonstrates quantitative inviscid damping of vertical components, and establishes global nonlinear stability under a suitable horizontal background magnetic field with a compatibility condition between field strength and dissipation coefficients.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand the stability and dynamics of MHD flows near shear flows under anisotropic dissipation (vertical-only viscosity and magnetic diffusivity), addressing important questions about enhanced dissipation, inviscid damping, and echo-type resonant interactions in a regime with a background magnetic field.
AI.method: The authors introduce shear-adapted Fourier multipliers that simultaneously capture three key effects: enhanced dissipation, critical-time effects, and echo-type resonant interactions. They analyze both the inviscid linearized problem and the nonlinear problem, imposing a horizontal background magnetic field and a quantitative compatibility condition between magnetic field strength, viscosity, and magnetic diffusivity.
AI.result: For the linearized inviscid problem with |β|>1/2: sharp linear-in-time growth of vorticity and current density is proven. Horizontal velocity and magnetic perturbations remain uniformly bounded, while vertical components exhibit inviscid damping at rate ⟨t⟩^{-1}. For the nonlinear problem: global nonlinear stability is established for H^N (N≥4) perturbations with size bounded by ε₀·min(μ,ν)^{1/2}, with nonzero horizontal Fourier modes decaying at enhanced-dissipation rate e^{-c·min(μ,ν)^{1/3}·t} and vertical components gaining an additional inviscid-damping factor ⟨t⟩^{-1}.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes rigorous stability results for anisotropic MHD near Couette flow, showing that background magnetic field and appropriate dissipation conditions lead to global stability with combined enhanced dissipation and inviscid damping mechanisms, even in the presence of transient linear growth induced by critical-time/echo-type effects.

title: Reduced Precision Diffusion Synthetic Acceleration for S$_N$ Neutron Transport in LLNL's ARDRA using Hypre
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, submitted to ANS M&C 2027
summary: Fast solution times in production discrete ordinates transport codes often require the use of diffusion synthetic acceleration (DSA). A good implementation of DSA will substantially reduce the number of iterations to converge the transport solution at the cost of solving a diffusion-like linear system at each iteration. Often fewer transport iterations will lead to smaller times to solution. Recent work has shown the promise of reduced precision preconditioning. Time and memory cost can be decreased as long as the reduced precision does not substantially degrade the convergence behavior of the higher precision linear system being solved. In this paper, we discuss the algorithmic implications of accelerating transport iterations in double precision (64 bit) while using a reduced precision (32 bit) DSA solve. We initially implement a stand alone code to investigate any theoretical limitations of reduced precision DSA in slabs. Then we implement reduced precision DSA in ARDRA, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's (LLNL) discrete ordinance neutral particle transport code, coupled with {\it hypre}, LLNL's scalable linear solver and multigrid methods library capable of mixed precision linear solves Then we solve various neutron transport problems of interest. We find that in most circumstances, DSA acceleration in reduced precision has little to no impact on the acceleration properties of DSA when used with source iteration in most circumstances. However, as tighter tolerances are required, reduced precision DSA may fail to successfully accelerate the transport solve and increase time to solution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the use of reduced precision (32-bit) diffusion synthetic acceleration (DSA) to accelerate double precision (64-bit) transport iterations in discrete ordinates codes. The authors implement reduced precision DSA both in a standalone slab code and in LLNL's ARDRA transport code coupled with the hypre library's mixed precision solvers. Results show reduced precision DSA generally preserves acceleration performance, though it may fail to accelerate and increase time to solution when tighter tolerances are required.
AI.motivation: DSA substantially reduces transport iteration counts but adds a diffusion-like linear solve per iteration. Recent work shows reduced precision preconditioning can decrease time and memory costs; this paper explores whether reduced precision DSA can accelerate double precision transport iterations without substantial degradation.
AI.method: The authors implement a standalone slab code to test theoretical limitations of reduced precision DSA, then integrate reduced precision DSA into ARDRA (LLNL's discrete ordinates transport code) coupled with hypre (LLNL's mixed precision linear solver library), and solve various neutron transport problems.
AI.result: Reduced precision DSA has little to no impact on acceleration properties of DSA with source iteration in most circumstances. However, when tighter tolerances are required, reduced precision DSA may fail to accelerate the transport solve, increasing time to solution.
AI.conclusion: Reduced precision (32-bit) DSA is largely effective for accelerating double precision transport iterations in most practical cases, but users must be cautious about tolerance requirements, as tightening tolerances can cause reduced precision DSA to lose its acceleration benefit.

title: Improving the efficiency of a Hyperpower method for approximating inverse matrices
summary: In this manuscript, scalar norm-type accelerators are used for first time in order to increase the order of convergence of known iterative methods for solving the matrix equation $X^{-1}-A=0$, while decreasing the number of matrix-matrix products. Specifically, our proposed scheme upgrades the order of convergence in a $50\%$, achieving the sixth-order of convergence with the computational cost of fourth-order Hyperpower method, in terms of matrix-matrix multiplications. In the main results, not only the convergence and its order is proven, but also its efficiency and stability. This new technique provides good numerical results, even compared with existing fourth-, sixth- and eighth-order schemes in large matrices of up to $10^6$ entries, but also promises the opening of a new kind of procedures with good performance and scalability. Finally, an application to digital image restoration is made to show the behavior of the method, compared with existing ones.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces scalar norm-type accelerators for the first time to improve iterative methods solving the matrix equation X^{-1}-A=0. The proposed scheme increases the order of convergence by 50% (reaching sixth-order) while maintaining the computational cost (in matrix-matrix multiplications) of the fourth-order Hyperpower method. Convergence, efficiency, and stability are proven, with numerical validation on large matrices up to 10^6 entries and an application to digital image restoration.
AI.motivation: To increase the order of convergence of existing iterative methods for computing matrix inverse (X^{-1}-A=0) while simultaneously reducing the number of matrix-matrix products, thereby improving computational efficiency.
AI.method: Scalar norm-type accelerators are applied for the first time to iterative schemes for matrix inversion. This accelerator technique upgrades the convergence order by 50%, achieving sixth-order convergence with the computational cost of the fourth-order Hyperpower method in terms of matrix-matrix multiplications.
AI.result: The method demonstrates proven convergence with sixth-order of convergence at the cost level of fourth-order methods. It delivers superior numerical results compared to existing fourth-, sixth-, and eighth-order schemes on large matrices up to 10^6 entries, and shows effective performance in digital image restoration applications.
AI.conclusion: The scalar norm-type acceleration technique opens a new class of procedures with good performance and scalability for matrix inversion, outperforming established higher-order methods in practice while maintaining lower computational cost.

title: Three asymptotic regimes for a Keller--Segel system with volume-filling effect
summary: We study three asymptotic regimes for a parabolic--elliptic Keller--Segel system with porous-medium diffusion and the volume-filling sensitivity function $u(1-u)$. First, when $D=ε^2\to0$, $δ=1$, $1\le m<2$, and the chemotactic sensitivity coefficient is below an explicit $m$-dependent parabolicity threshold, we prove strong convergence to a scalar nonlinear diffusion equation. Second, as $δ=ε\to0$ with $D=1$, we obtain a hyperbolic--elliptic Keller--Segel limit by means of a kinetic reduction argument. Third, under the scaling $χ=ε^{-1}$, $D=ε^2$, $δ=1$, and for characteristic initial data of finite perimeter, we prove convergence on fixed time intervals to the time-independent initial patch in $BV(Ω;\{0,1\})$. Because the sensitivity function is nonlinear in the density, weak convergence alone is insufficient to identify the chemotactic flux. Strong compactness of the density is therefore required in all three regimes and is obtained, respectively, through energy--entropy estimates, kinetic reduction, and $BV$ compactness.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes three distinct asymptotic regimes of a parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system with porous-medium diffusion and volume-filling sensitivity u(1-u), proving convergence to: (1) a scalar nonlinear diffusion equation, (2) a hyperbolic-elliptic Keller-Segel limit, and (3) the initial patch via BV compactness.
AI.motivation: The study of asymptotic regimes is essential for understanding the various limiting behaviors of the Keller-Segel chemotaxis model. Since the sensitivity function is nonlinear in density, weak convergence alone cannot identify the chemotactic flux, necessitating new analytical strategies to establish strong compactness of the density.
AI.method: The paper employs three distinct analytical strategies corresponding to each regime: (1) energy-entropy estimates for the ε²→0 diffusion scaling with an explicit m-dependent parabolicity threshold; (2) a kinetic reduction argument for the δ→0 limit; (3) BV compactness for the χ=ε⁻¹, D=ε² scaling with finite-perimeter characteristic initial data.
AI.result: The paper proves strong convergence of the density in all three asymptotic regimes: to a scalar nonlinear diffusion equation below the parabolicity threshold, to a hyperbolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system, and to the initial patch in BV(Ω;{0,1}) on fixed time intervals.
AI.conclusion: Strong compactness of the density—achieved through different mechanisms (energy-entropy, kinetic reduction, or BV compactness)—is the key required tool to identify the nonlinear chemotactic flux in all three asymptotic limits.

title: Learning multistate kinetics with a variational multistate committor network
summary: The long-time dynamics of complex molecular systems often involves rare transitions across networks of metastable states. Building on transition-path theory, which provides a rigorous framework for describing rare transitions between two metastable states, we introduce the variational multistate committor network (VMCN), a neural framework that learns the probabilities of reaching each metastable state directly from molecular simulation data. From this representation, VMCN identifies state-specific commitment, candidate transition regions and committor-consistent pathways between state pairs, and an effective kinetic network characterized by transition rates. The model is trained using finite time-lag trajectory data together with boundary conditions defined on conservative state cores. Applications to a triple-well potential, trialanine isomerization, and the $c$--ring rotation in the V$_{\rm o}$ domain of a vacuolar ATPase show that VMCN recovers metastable organization, provides committor-consistent descriptions of transition mechanisms, and estimates state-to-state kinetics. VMCN further provides diagnostics for incomplete state decompositions and enables adaptive exploration of candidate metastable states and their connecting regions. By integrating VMCN with generative committor-guided path sampling (Gen-COMPAS) for chignolin, we start from two end point structures, identify a misfolded state and a candidate folding intermediate, and we direct subsequent sampling toward the resulting multistate transition network.

AI.tldr: VMCN is a neural framework that learns multistate committor probabilities from molecular simulation data, enabling identification of metastable states, transition pathways, and kinetic networks from trajectory data alone.
AI.motivation: Complex molecular systems exhibit rare transitions across networks of metastable states, and existing transition-path theory frameworks primarily address two-state transitions, lacking a general approach for multistate systems that directly learns committor probabilities from simulation data.
AI.method: VMCN trains a neural network to learn probabilities of reaching each metastable state using finite time-lag trajectory data with boundary conditions on conservative state cores. From this learned representation, it extracts state-specific commitment functions, transition regions, committor-consistent pathways, and an effective kinetic network with transition rates.
AI.result: Applications to a triple-well potential, trialanine isomerization, and c-ring rotation in the Vo domain of a vacuolar ATPase demonstrate VMCN recovers metastable organization, provides committor-consistent transition mechanisms, and estimates state-to-state kinetics. When combined with Gen-COMPAS for chignolin folding, VMCN identified a misfolded state and a candidate folding intermediate from only two endpoint structures.
AI.conclusion: VMCN provides diagnostics for incomplete state decompositions, enables adaptive exploration of candidate metastable states, and integrates with generative path-sampling methods to guide sampling toward multistate transition networks, offering a general tool for characterizing rare-event dynamics in molecular systems.

title: Adaptive Multilevel Discontinuous Galerkin Methods on GPUs
summary: I present a matrix-free symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method for adaptively refined Cartesian meshes on GPUs. At non-matching interfaces, auxiliary \emph{shadow cells} represent the adjacent coarse polynomial on the fine level. This approach converts non-matching interfaces into matching faces, permitting uniform face evaluation throughout the mesh. I prove that this construction is equivalent to the standard non-matching formulation. Furthermore, this representation yields a local geometric multigrid method in which frozen shadows provide inter-level boundary data and carry residual contributions to coarser levels. A primal--dual pairing eliminates shadow assembly from the Krylov iteration. Numerical experiments with cubic elements ($p=3$) on an NVIDIA A100 show stable multigrid convergence under increasing refinement depth and efficient GPU execution.

AI.tldr: A matrix-free symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method for adaptively refined Cartesian meshes on GPUs, using shadow cells to convert non-matching interfaces into matching faces, enabling uniform face evaluation and a local geometric multigrid solver.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient GPU implementation of discontinuous Galerkin methods on adaptively refined (non-conforming) Cartesian meshes, where non-matching interfaces complicate face evaluation and solver design.
AI.method: Introduces shadow cells at non-matching interfaces to represent adjacent coarse polynomials on the fine level, converting non-matching interfaces into matching faces. Proves equivalence to standard non-matching formulation. This enables a local geometric multigrid method where frozen shadows provide inter-level boundary data and carry residuals to coarser levels. A primal-dual pairing avoids shadow assembly in Krylov iterations.
AI.result: Numerical experiments with cubic elements (p=3) on an NVIDIA A100 demonstrate stable multigrid convergence under increasing refinement depth and efficient GPU execution.
AI.conclusion: The shadow-cell representation provides an equivalent, GPU-friendly formulation of non-matching DG interfaces that enables efficient multigrid solvers on adaptively refined Cartesian meshes.

title: On Liouville problems for $(p,q)$-Laplacian inequalities on Finsler measure spaces
summary: We study the Liouville property for nonnegative weak solutions of the $(p,q)$-Laplacian elliptic differential inequality $$Δ^{m}_{p}u(x)+Δ^{m}_{q}u(x)+V(x)u^{s}(x)\leq 0$$ and the associated parabolic differential inequality $$\partial_t u(x,t) \geq Δ^{m}_{p}u(x,t)+Δ^{m}_{q}u(x,t)+V(x,t)u^{s}(x,t)$$ on a forward geodesically complete noncompact Finsler measure space $(M,F,m)$ with finite reversibility. Under several sets of integral growth conditions on the positive potential function over certain annular domains, we prove that any nonnegative weak solution vanishes almost everywhere. The proofs of our results are essentially based on the nonlinear capacity method.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the Liouville property (non-existence of nontrivial nonnegative weak solutions) for elliptic and parabolic (p,q)-Laplacian differential inequalities with potentials on forward geodesically complete noncompact Finsler measure spaces of finite reversibility. Using the nonlinear capacity method, the authors prove that nonnegative weak solutions vanish almost everywhere under various integral growth conditions on the potential over annular domains.
AI.motivation: To extend the study of Liouville-type theorems from Euclidean/Riemannian settings to general Finsler measure spaces, specifically for the (p,q)-Laplacian with potential terms in both elliptic and parabolic inequalities.
AI.method: The proofs rely on the nonlinear capacity method, applied on forward geodesically complete noncompact Finsler measure spaces with finite reversibility, under integral growth conditions on the positive potential over annular domains.
AI.result: Under several sets of integral growth conditions on the positive potential, every nonnegative weak solution to the given elliptic and parabolic (p,q)-Laplacian inequalities vanishes almost everywhere.
AI.conclusion: The results establish Liouville-type vanishing theorems for (p,q)-Laplacian inequalities on Finsler measure spaces, generalizing prior work to a broader geometric setting via the nonlinear capacity approach.

title: Learning Memory-Dependent Neural Network Correlation Potentials for Accurate Electron Dynamics
summary: Time-dependent density functional theory, though exact in theory, is in practice applied in an adiabatic approximation using exchange-correlation functionals with only local temporal dependence. Simultaneously, the exact correlation potential formally depends on, among other quantities, the time-history of electron densities. Here we develop a framework to learn neural network models of correlation functionals that feature explicit memory-dependence. Our framework includes two different approaches, both linked through their use of adjoint-based optimization. One approach decouples the learning of the functional from inversion to find ground truth values of the correlation potential. The other approach learns the functional directly without requiring inversion. We apply these methods to modeling the electron dynamics of two-electron systems in two spatial dimensions. In both cases, our methods yield correlation functionals with low test set propagation error, outperforming standard local density and generalized gradient approximation functionals by one to two orders of magnitude. Overall, our framework points at one strategy to move beyond the adiabatic approximation and develop memory-dependent correlation functionals that yield accurate propagation for excited state and/or non-equilibrium dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a neural network framework for learning memory-dependent correlation functionals in time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT), moving beyond the standard adiabatic approximation. Two adjoint-optimization-based approaches are presented: one that decouples functional learning from inversion, and another that learns directly without inversion. Applied to two-electron systems in 2D, both methods achieve correlation functionals with test set propagation errors one to two orders of magnitude lower than standard local density and GGA functionals.
AI.motivation: TDDFT is exact in theory but applied practically through the adiabatic approximation with exchange-correlation functionals having only local temporal dependence. However, the exact correlation potential formally depends on the time-history of electron densities (memory effects). This discrepancy limits accuracy for excited state and non-equilibrium dynamics, motivating the need for memory-dependent correlation functionals.
AI.method: The framework uses neural networks to represent correlation functionals with explicit memory dependence. Two approaches are developed, both leveraging adjoint-based optimization: (1) one approach decouples functional learning from inversion to obtain ground truth values of the correlation potential, and (2) another learns the functional directly without requiring inversion. Both are applied to model electron dynamics of two-electron systems in two spatial dimensions.
AI.result: Both methods produce correlation functionals with low test set propagation error, outperforming standard local density approximation (LDA) and generalized gradient approximation (GGA) functionals by one to two orders of magnitude in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a viable strategy to move beyond the adiabatic approximation, enabling the development of memory-dependent correlation functionals that yield accurate propagation for excited state and/or non-equilibrium dynamics in TDDFT.

title: A Complete Resolution of Forsythe's Conjecture for Restarted Conjugate Gradients
summary: Forsythe's conjecture, published in 1968, asserts that for each restart length $s$, every exact-arithmetic restarted conjugate-gradient iteration on a real symmetric positive definite problem either terminates or has normalised residuals that converge separately along the even and odd restart subsequences. Apart from the classical steepest-descent case, this asymptotic question remained unresolved in full generality for nearly six decades. We give a complete classification by restart length in the original finite-dimensional setting and identify a sharp threshold. For $s=2$ and $s=3$, every problem either terminates or has convergent even and odd residual directions. For every $s\ge4$, there is a diagonal positive definite counterexample of dimension $s+4$ which never terminates and whose even residual directions do not converge. Together with Akaike's theorem for $s=1$, this shows that the conjectured universal conclusion is true precisely for $s\in\{1,2,3\}$ and false for every $s\ge4$. The positive results follow from a degree-independent double-orthogonality identity and an analysis of the low-degree fixed-point sets. At restart length four, rational interval arithmetic and Sturm sequences certify a transverse Hopf point of the leading vector field of the rescaled squared-weight map. Analytic periodic-orbit and shadowing arguments yield the counterexample at restart length four, and degree elevation extends the construction to every larger restart length.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves Forsythe's 1968 conjecture on restarted conjugate-gradient iterations by giving a complete classification: the conjecture holds exactly for restart lengths s∈{1,2,3} and fails for every s≥4, where explicit diagonal counterexamples exist.
AI.motivation: Forsythe's conjecture from 1968 about convergence of normalized residuals in restarted conjugate-gradient iterations remained unresolved in full generality for nearly six decades (except the classical steepest-descent case, i.e., s=1 via Akaike's theorem). The authors aim to settle this long-standing open question.
AI.method: The paper uses a combination of techniques: (1) a degree-independent double-orthogonality identity and analysis of low-degree fixed-point sets for the positive results at s=2 and s=3; (2) at restart length s=4, rational interval arithmetic and Sturm sequences to certify a transverse Hopf point of the leading vector field of the rescaled squared-weight map; (3) analytic periodic-orbit and shadowing arguments to construct the counterexample at s=4; (4) degree elevation to extend the construction to all s≥4.
AI.result: A sharp threshold is identified: for s=2 and s=3 every problem terminates or has convergent even and odd residual directions; for every s≥4 there exists a diagonal positive definite counterexample of dimension s+4 that never terminates and whose even residual directions diverge. Together with Akaike's theorem for s=1, Forsythe's conjectured universal conclusion holds precisely for s∈{1,2,3} and fails for every s≥4.
AI.conclusion: Forsythe's conjecture is settled with a complete classification by restart length, revealing a sharp threshold at s=4. The conjecture is true precisely for restart lengths 1, 2, and 3, and false for all s≥4.

title: On smooth inviscid vortices with fat tails
summary: We derive a family of degenerate vortices with non trivial swirls and fat tails which can be used to bifurcate both stationary and self similar solutions to the three dimensional axi-symmetric incompressible Euler equations.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a family of degenerate vortices with non-trivial swirl and fat tails, which serve as bifurcation points for both stationary and self-similar solutions to the 3D axi-symmetric incompressible Euler equations.
AI.motivation: To find constructible degenerate vortex solutions that can act as bifurcation points for generating new stationary and self-similar solutions of the 3D axi-symmetric Euler equations, potentially enriching the understanding of vortex structures in ideal fluids.
AI.method: The authors derive a family of degenerate vortices characterized by non-trivial swirl components and fat (slowly decaying) tails, and use these as base states to bifurcate both stationary and self-similar solutions of the axi-symmetric incompressible Euler system.
AI.result: A family of degenerate vortices with non-trivial swirls and fat tails is explicitly derived, and it is shown that both stationary and self-similar solutions can be bifurcated from these degenerate vortex configurations.
AI.conclusion: Degenerate vortices with swirl and fat tails provide a versatile framework for generating both stationary and self-similar solutions to the 3D axi-symmetric incompressible Euler equations via bifurcation.

title: An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics
summary: We develop an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. Motivated by the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, the latent vector field is generated from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator and a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. This potential is learned in nonunique latent coordinates and is not identified with the Gibbs free energy, but decreases monotonically along autonomous continuous-time solutions, while the antisymmetric component permits motion along its level sets. The encoder, decoder, latent energy, and operators are trained jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses alone, without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, an initial state is encoded once, evolved in latent space, and decoded only at the requested output times, enabling substantially cheaper trajectory prediction than the micromagnetic solver used to generate the training data. We compare quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic latent energies on two datasets parameterized by field amplitude and generated for the two applied-field directions of the NIST $μ$MAG Standard Problem 4. Dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models achieve comparable accuracy on short training-style windows but differ substantially on uninterrupted rollouts, for which the antisymmetric-dissipative models provide markedly more accurate trajectory predictions. The deep-quadratic energy gives the best overall accuracy for both field directions and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic dynamics, combining a convolutional autoencoder with a structured latent neural ODE that decomposes the latent vector field into precessional (antisymmetric) and dissipative (symmetric) components derived from a learned scalar potential. Models are trained on short trajectory windows without physical-energy labels or dissipation penalties, and the antisymmetric-dissipative architecture with deep-quadratic energy provides the most accurate long-horizon trajectory predictions.
AI.motivation: To enable substantially cheaper trajectory prediction than full micromagnetic solvers by learning a reduced-order latent dynamical model that respects the underlying precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation.
AI.method: A convolutional autoencoder maps micromagnetic states to latent coordinates; a structured neural ODE evolves these latent states. The latent vector field is built from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator (precession) and a symmetric positive-semidefinite operator (dissipation). The encoder, decoder, potential, and operators are jointly trained using only latent and decoded-rollout losses on short trajectory windows, without time-derivative supervision or physical energy labels. Three energy forms (quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic) are compared.
AI.result: On NIST µMAG Standard Problem 4 datasets for both field directions: dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models perform comparably on short training-style windows but differ on uninterrupted rollouts, where antisymmetric-dissipative models are markedly more accurate. The deep-quadratic energy achieves the best overall accuracy for both field directions and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing the precessional-dissipative structure in the latent dynamics significantly improves long-horizon prediction accuracy, and the deep-quadratic latent energy is the most effective parameterization among those tested.

title: A class of high-order discontinuous-Galerkin methods satisfying infinitely many entropy conditions with provable error estimates and strong convergence for general nonlinear conservation laws
summary: We propose a novel framework for deriving semi-discrete discontinuous-Galerkin (DG) methods using operator semigroups for scalar conservation laws, then apply it to construct a class of high-order OFDG-type schemes [13] satisfying infinitely many local entropy inequalities with general E-fluxes on non-uniform meshes. Such schemes are further generalized to systems of conservation laws in any number of space dimensions by using entropy stable numerical fluxes in the sense of [1]. Finally, we prove optimal error estimates for smooth solutions to nonlinear scalar conservation laws, and prove strong convergence for discontinuous solutions to strictly convex conservation laws via compensated compactness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel framework for deriving semi-discrete discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods via operator semigroups for scalar conservation laws. It constructs high-order OFDG-type schemes satisfying infinitely many local entropy inequalities with general E-fluxes on non-uniform meshes, extends them to systems of conservation laws in any space dimension using entropy stable numerical fluxes, and proves optimal error estimates for smooth solutions and strong convergence for discontinuous solutions via compensated compactness.
AI.motivation: The goal is to develop a general theoretical framework for DG methods for conservation laws that guarantees entropy stability (via infinitely many local entropy inequalities), extends to systems in multiple dimensions, and provides rigorous convergence/error estimates for both smooth and discontinuous solutions.
AI.method: The authors use operator semigroup theory to derive semi-discrete DG methods, then apply this to build high-order OFDG-type schemes. The schemes incorporate general E-fluxes on non-uniform meshes to satisfy infinitely many local entropy inequalities. For systems, entropy stable numerical fluxes are used, and analysis employs compensated compactness techniques for discontinuous solutions.
AI.result: Optimal error estimates are proved for smooth solutions of nonlinear scalar conservation laws, and strong convergence is established for discontinuous solutions to strictly convex conservation laws via compensated compactness.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous foundation for constructing entropy-stable high-order DG-type schemes for conservation laws, with proven convergence properties in both smooth and discontinuous regimes.

title: Failure of analyticity-radius growth in energy-canceling fluid models
summary:
We prove that exact quadratic energy cancellation alone does not force growth of the spatial analyticity radius. On $\mathbb{T}^3$, we construct an explicit symmetric, translation-invariant, first-order bilinear operator $Q$ that preserves the divergence-free class and, for every smooth real-valued divergence-free vector field $v$, satisfies $ \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} Q(v,v)\cdot v\,dx=0.$ For every prescribed sufficiently small time $T>0$, the equation $\partial_t u-Δu=Q(u,u)$ admits a global smooth, real-valued, mean-zero, divergence-free solution $u$ such that $\operatorname{rad}(u(0))=\operatorname{rad}(u(T))=1$. The construction reduces the dynamics on an invariant cyclic-shear class to viscous Burgers and tunes a Cole-Hopf heat profile so that its nearest complex zero returns to its initial distance from the real torus.
  For every $1<α<2$ and every prescribed sufficiently small $T>0$, we also construct a symmetric sparse frequency set, its associated Fourier projection, and trigonometric-polynomial initial data for the projected dissipative surface quasi-geostrophic equation. The resulting unique global smooth solution $θ$ has infinite analyticity radius initially but satisfies $0<\operatorname{rad}(θ(T))\leq1$. An additively separated Fourier cascade yields coefficientwise exponential lower bounds, while uniform comparison estimates control the feedback interactions. Thus entire analyticity need not persist even from trigonometric-polynomial data. Together, the two constructions show that an exact energy identity alone does not determine the frequency geometry governing analyticity-radius growth.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs explicit counterexamples showing that exact quadratic energy cancellation alone does not determine the growth of spatial analyticity radius. Two constructions are given: (1) a divergence-free bilinear operator on T³ with exact energy identity whose equation admits solutions whose analyticity radius stays at 1 over arbitrary small times, and (2) a projected dissipative surface quasi-geostrophic equation with trigonometric-polynomial data whose solution loses entire analyticity (infinite radius becomes finite within any prescribed short time).
AI.motivation: A natural question in hydrodynamic PDE theory is whether exact energy cancellation (a formal energy identity) is sufficient to guarantee persistence or growth of the spatial analyticity radius, which is central to understanding well-posedness and regularity. The authors seek to determine whether energy structure alone dictates analyticity-radius behavior or whether frequency geometry plays an independent role.
AI.method: The first construction reduces the dynamics of a carefully chosen symmetric, translation-invariant, first-order bilinear operator on an invariant cyclic-shear class to viscous Burgers. A Cole-Hopf heat profile is tuned so its nearest complex zero returns to its initial distance from the real torus, keeping the analyticity radius fixed at 1. The second construction builds a symmetric sparse frequency set, a Fourier projection, and trigonometric-polynomial initial data for a projected dissipative surface quasi-geostrophic equation. An additively separated Fourier cascade yields coefficientwise exponential lower bounds, while uniform comparison estimates control feedback interactions.
AI.result: For every sufficiently small prescribed T>0, the energy-conserving equation on T³ admits global smooth solutions with analyticity radius exactly 1 at both initial and final times (exact energy identity but no radius growth). For 1<α<2, projected dissipative SQG equations admit solutions starting from trigonometric polynomials (infinite analyticity radius) that nonetheless have finite bounded analyticity radius at time T, showing entire analyticity need not persist. Both constructions work for all sufficiently small prescribed times.
AI.conclusion: Exact energy identities alone do not determine the frequency geometry governing analyticity-radius growth or persistence. Additional structural/dynamical information about the operator's frequency interactions is essential to predict analyticity behavior, isolating energy cancellation as an insufficient criterion for radius growth.

title: Energy-Consistent Splitting and Decomposition Approaches for Coupled port-Hamiltonian ODEs
summary: Operator splitting provides an attractive approach for the numerical integration of (coupled) port-Hamiltonian systems, as it allows the underlying system structure to be exploited at the level of the individual subproblems. However, the choice of the decomposition is not unique and may strongly affect both the computational efficiency and the preservation of the energy behavior of the original system. In this work, we investigate this interplay systematically and introduce energy consistency as a criterion for assessing splitting methods for port-Hamiltonian ordinary differential equations. We derive sufficient conditions under which a splitting based on a given decomposition inherits the energy behavior of the continuous system and use these conditions to analyze several decomposition strategies for coupled port-Hamiltonian systems. In particular, we compare decompositions that preserve the structure with approaches that exploit lower-dimensional subsystem dynamics or separated time scales. The analysis is complemented by numerical experiments using Strang splitting and its multiple-time-stepping extension. A scalable electro-thermal benchmark with fast electrical and slow thermal dynamics is employed to assess accuracy, energy behavior, and computational efficiency. The results demonstrate that preserving the port-Hamiltonian structure of the subflows is essential for energy-consistent splitting, whereas decompositions that exploit subsystem structure or time-scale separation can provide substantial computational advantages. In particular, the time-scale decomposition yields significant efficiency gains for systems with pronounced multirate characteristics, while structure-destroying decompositions may lead to undesirable energy behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates operator splitting methods for port-Hamiltonian systems, introducing "energy consistency" as a criterion to assess whether different decompositions preserve the energy behavior of the original coupled system. The authors derive sufficient conditions for energy-consistent splitting and compare structure-preserving decompositions against those exploiting lower-dimensional subsystems or time-scale separation, using a scalable electro-thermal benchmark with Strang splitting.
AI.motivation: Operator splitting for port-Hamiltonian systems allows exploitation of system structure at the subproblem level, but the decomposition choice is non-unique and can strongly affect both computational efficiency and energy preservation. There is a need for a systematic criterion to evaluate and compare different splitting strategies for coupled port-Hamiltonian systems.
AI.method: The authors (1) introduce energy consistency as a criterion for assessing splitting methods for port-Hamiltonian ODEs, (2) derive sufficient conditions under which a splitting based on a given decomposition inherits the continuous system's energy behavior, (3) use these conditions to analyze various decomposition strategies for coupled systems (structure-preserving, subsystem-exploiting, and time-scale-separated decompositions), and (4) validate with numerical experiments using Strang splitting and its multiple-time-stepping extension on an electro-thermal benchmark.
AI.result: Structure-preserving decompositions of subflows are essential for energy-consistent splitting. Decompositions exploiting subsystem structure or time-scale separation offer substantial computational advantages—particularly time-scale decomposition for systems with pronounced multirate characteristics—while structure-destroying decompositions can lead to undesirable energy behavior.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a fundamental trade-off: preserving port-Hamiltonian structure in subflows is critical for energy consistency, but decomposing based on physical subsystems or time scales can yield significant efficiency gains. The derived criteria provide a principled framework for selecting decompositions that balance energy fidelity and computational cost.

title: A dispersive extension result for a class of nonlocal nonlinearities
summary: We prove that a class of nonlocal nonlinearities on periodic Sobolev spaces can be expressed as a trace of the unique mild solution to a local dispersive problem consisting of a system of forced Schrödinger equations. The proof is based on a reformulation of the nonlocal nonlinearities as the resonant orbit average of a real-analytic function under the unitary group generated by the free Schrödinger operator $\mathrm{i} \partial_x^2$. We illustrate our result by providing an equivalent local reformulation for a recently obtained nonlocal amplitude equation that formally captures the dynamics of parabolic systems close to a conserved Hopf instability.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that certain nonlocal nonlinearities on periodic Sobolev spaces can be expressed as traces of unique mild solutions to a local system of forced Schrödinger equations, using a reformulation of the nonlocal terms as resonant orbit averages under the free Schrödinger unitary group. The result is illustrated by providing an equivalent local reformulation of a nonlocal amplitude equation relevant to parabolic systems near a conserved Hopf instability.
AI.motivation: To bridge nonlocal and local descriptions of nonlinear dynamics, showing that seemingly nonlocal nonlinear terms on periodic Sobolev spaces can be equivalently encoded through a local dispersive system of forced Schrödinger equations — enabling the use of local techniques for nonlocal problems.
AI.method: The proof relies on expressing the nonlocal nonlinearities as the resonant orbit average of a real-analytic function under the unitary group generated by the free Schrödinger operator i∂²x, thereby linking them to the trace of a unique mild solution of a local system of forced Schrödinger equations.
AI.result: The authors establish the equivalence theorem and demonstrate its applicability by deriving an equivalent local reformulation for a previously obtained nonlocal amplitude equation that formally describes parabolic systems near a conserved Hopf instability.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal nonlinearities in periodic Sobolev settings can be rigorously recast as local dispersive problems, a connection that may facilitate new analytical tools for such systems.

title: Voltage-embedded equivariant machine learning potential for open system simulations
summary: Modeling electrochemical interfaces under operational non-equilibrium conditions is vital for energy technologies but remains bottlenecked by the expensive cost of ab initio methods. Current machine learning potentials, largely designed for closed systems under homogeneous electric fields, are limited in open quantum transport applications. To overcome this, we present an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network that embeds voltage bias for open-system simulations. Our approach decouples the system energy and forces into zero-bias and bias-dependent contributions, assigning distinct vector encodings to electrode and scattering-region atoms to capture non-equilibrium conditions. Trained on limited discrete bias data, the model achieves high predictive accuracy and robust extrapolation transferability. When applied to a lithium/water interface, our model successfully captures the field-induced dynamic reorientation of water molecules and reproduces asymmetric electrochemical behavior at different electrodes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network (GNN) that embeds voltage bias for modeling electrochemical interfaces under non-equilibrium (open-system) conditions. The model decouples system energy/forces into zero-bias and bias-dependent components with distinct vector encodings for electrode and scattering-region atoms, achieving high accuracy and extrapolation on limited training data. Demonstrated on a lithium/water interface, it captures field-induced water reorientation and asymmetric electrode behavior.
AI.motivation: Modeling electrochemical interfaces under operational non-equilibrium conditions is critical for energy technologies, but ab initio methods are prohibitively expensive. Existing machine learning potentials are designed for closed systems under homogeneous electric fields and cannot handle open quantum transport applications with voltage bias.
AI.method: An E(3)-equivariant graph neural network that embeds voltage bias for open-system simulations. The approach decouples system energy and forces into zero-bias and bias-dependent contributions, and assigns distinct vector encodings to electrode versus scattering-region atoms to capture non-equilibrium conditions. The model is trained on limited discrete bias data.
AI.result: The model achieves high predictive accuracy and robust extrapolation transferability despite limited training data. Applied to a lithium/water interface, it successfully captures field-induced dynamic reorientation of water molecules and reproduces asymmetric electrochemical behavior at different electrodes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed equivariant GNN with bias embedding provides an efficient and accurate machine learning framework for modeling electrochemical interfaces under non-equilibrium open-system conditions, overcoming the limitations of existing closed-system machine learning potentials.

title: Construction of trace-preserving Fortin operators
summary: We present a unifying framework to construct local Fortin operators for conforming mixed finite element pairs for the Stokes equations. The operators are constructed to satisfy the divergence-preservation property, local stability and approximation properties, and certain trace-preservation properties. For the latter, some of the finite element pairs require an enrichment of the velocity space. We present the construction for the $P_d-P_0$ element, the Bernardi-Raugel element, the conforming Crouzeix-Raviart element, a modified MINI element and generalised Taylor-Hood elements. Furthermore, we discuss implications of the existence of such a Fortin operator beyond inf-sup stability. These include applications to non-Newtonian fluid flow, problems with inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, as well as uniform inf-sup stability relevant for domain approximation and moving domains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified framework for constructing local Fortin operators for conforming mixed finite element pairs used in Stokes equations, covering several classic elements (P_d-P_0, Bernardi-Raugel, Crouzeix-Raviart, MINI, Taylor-Hood) and discussing applications beyond basic inf-sup stability.
AI.motivation: Fortin operators are essential for proving inf-sup stability of mixed finite element methods, but their construction is often element-specific and ad hoc. A unified framework would simplify analysis and extend applicability to more complex problems.
AI.method: The authors construct local Fortin operators satisfying divergence-preservation, local stability, approximation properties, and trace-preservation properties. Some finite element pairs require velocity space enrichment. The framework is applied to P_d-P_0, Bernardi-Raugel, conforming Crouzeix-Raviart, modified MINI, and generalized Taylor-Hood elements.
AI.result: The unified framework successfully constructs Fortin operators for all listed element pairs, with velocity enrichment needed for certain trace-preservation requirements. The implications extend to non-Newtonian flows, inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, and uniform inf-sup stability for domain approximation and moving domains.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a general, unifying construction of Fortin operators that goes beyond standard inf-sup stability, enabling applications to broader classes of flow problems and domain-dependent settings.

title: Monotonicity formulas in positively curved settings with applications to two-phase free boundary problems
summary: Inspired by the monotonicity formula of Alt, Caffarelli, and Friedman, we consider a natural variant of the ACF functional in positively curved 2-dimensional settings where we integrate over sublevel sets of Green's function rather than disks. We prove sharp almost-monotonicity formulas for our new functional in the case of convex planar domains (both with the pole on the boundary and in the interior) and in the setting of 2-dimensional complete manifolds with Euclidean volume growth and nonnegative Gaussian curvature. The tools include the Schwarz-Christoffel formula and Riesz decomposition using conformal coordinates. As a consequence, using quasiconformal estimates, we give a new Lipschitz bound in the manifold setting for minimizers of the two-phase free boundary problem of Alt, Caffarelli, and Friedman, with the constant depending on only the total integral curvature, in contrast to work of Teixeira and Zhang, which gives constants depending on pointwise bounds for the Riemann curvature tensor and its derivatives. Our methods also recover the Lipschitz bound up to a Neumann boundary of Gemmer, Moon, and Raynor in the planar convex domain case.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a new variant of the Alt-Caffarelli-Friedman (ACF) functional for positively curved 2D settings, integrating over Green's function sublevel sets instead of disks, and proves sharp almost-monotonicity formulas in convex planar domains and 2D manifolds with nonnegative Gaussian curvature, yielding new Lipschitz bounds for free boundary problem minimizers.
AI.motivation: The ACF monotonicity formula is a foundational tool in free boundary problems, but its classical form relies on Euclidean structure. The authors seek a natural adaptation to positively curved 2D settings, aiming to improve Lipschitz regularity results by removing dependence on pointwise curvature bounds and their derivatives.
AI.method: The approach introduces a Green's function-based variant of the ACF functional, using sublevel sets of Green's function in place of Euclidean disks. Tools include the Schwarz-Christoffel formula, Riesz decomposition in conformal coordinates, and quasiconformal estimates to derive the monotonicity and Lipschitz bounds across different geometric settings.
AI.result: Sharp almost-monotonicity formulas are proven for convex planar domains (pole on boundary or interior) and 2D complete manifolds with Euclidean volume growth and nonnegative Gaussian curvature. A new Lipschitz bound is obtained for minimizers of the two-phase ACF free boundary problem, with the constant depending only on total integral curvature rather than pointwise curvature bounds, and the planar convex case recovers the earlier Lipschitz bound of Gemmer, Moon, and Raynor.
AI.conclusion: The Green's function-based ACF functional provides a powerful framework for extending monotonicity and regularity results to positively curved settings, yielding geometric (rather than pointwise) curvature dependence and recovering previous work in the planar case.

title: FUSION: a skill-based research agent for publicly obtainable nuclear-physics codes
comment: 11 pages, 10 figures. Platform at https://github.com/jinleiphys/FUSION (MIT), documentation at https://vibeinscience.com
summary: Running an unfamiliar nuclear-physics code is rarely difficult because of the physics alone. One must find and build the program, learn its input conventions, and decide whether a plausible output is actually correct. A general-purpose coding agent helps with the first two tasks but may make the last one harder: it can write an input file that runs with the wrong physical convention. FUSION addresses this problem with code-specific skills. A skill obtains the code from its public source, starts from a verified input, runs and parses the calculation, records known failure modes, and must reproduce a stated benchmark to a stated tolerance before reporting a result. The current release covers twenty codes, spanning optical models and reactions, nuclear structure, fission and statistical models, astrophysics and R-matrix analysis, and heavy-ion transport. It also includes an offline, searchable collection of 61 167 pages derived from the nucl-th literature. User notes and credentials remain outside the public repository. FUSION is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/jinleiphys/FUSION; documentation is at https://vibeinscience.com. Here I describe the design, the checks behind the current release, and one complete calculation from input to comparison with measured data.

AI.tldr: FUSION is a framework that adds code-specific skills to general-purpose coding agents for nuclear-physics computation, ensuring physically correct usage of unfamiliar codes through verified benchmarks and version-controlled input conventions.
AI.motivation: Running unfamiliar nuclear-physics codes is challenging not just due to physics but due to finding/building the program, learning input conventions, and verifying output correctness. Coding agents help with the first two but can introduce errors by using wrong physical conventions when writing input files.
AI.method: FUSION employs code-specific skills: each skill fetches code from public sources, starts from verified inputs, runs/parses calculations, records known failure modes, and requires reproduction of a stated benchmark within a stated tolerance before reporting results. The release covers twenty codes across multiple nuclear-physics domains and includes an offline searchable collection of 61,167 pages from nucl-th literature.
AI.result: Current release covers twenty codes spanning optical models/reactions, nuclear structure, fission/statistical models, astrophysics, R-matrix analysis, and heavy-ion transport, plus an offline literature collection. One complete calculation from input to comparison with measured data is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: FUSION addresses the reliability gap in agent-driven nuclear-physics computation by embedding physical validation into the workflow, keeping user credentials private, and is released open-source under MIT license.

title: Frequency-explicit convergence analysis of a multiscale finite element method for highly heterogeneous scattering problems
summary: We analyze the numerical approximation of time-harmonic scattering by highly heterogeneous penetrable obstacles. These problems are especially challenging in the high-frequency regime, where the size of the scatterer $L$ is much larger than the wavelength, i.e., the wavenumber $k$ is such that $kL \gg 1$. Here, we further consider the situation where the scatterer contains different materials, with a characteristic size $\varepsilon$ such that $k\varepsilon \ll 1$. We propose a high-order multiscale finite element method, and provide an error analysis that is explicit in both $k$ and $\varepsilon$. Crucially, our error estimates suggest that using a high-order method should reduce the computational cost for large frequencies, which is corroborated by numerical examples.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a high-order multiscale finite element method for time-harmonic scattering problems involving highly heterogeneous penetrable obstacles, with error analysis explicitly dependent on both wavenumber k and material scale ε, demonstrating computational savings at high frequencies.
AI.motivation: Time-harmonic scattering by heterogeneous penetrable obstacles is notoriously difficult in the high-frequency regime (kL >> 1) and becomes even more challenging when the scatterer contains fine-scale material variations (kε << 1). Standard methods either fail or become prohibitively expensive in this two-scale setting.
AI.method: A high-order multiscale finite element method is proposed that handles both the large-scale (oscillatory wave behavior) and small-scale (material heterogeneity) features. The method is accompanied by an error analysis that is explicit in both the wavenumber k and the heterogeneity scale ε.
AI.result: Error estimates indicate that higher-order methods reduce computational cost for large frequencies. Numerical examples confirm this predicted advantage of high-order approaches.
AI.conclusion: High-order multiscale finite element methods offer an effective and theoretically justified strategy for high-frequency scattering from heterogeneous materials, with demonstrated computational efficiency gains at large wavenumbers.

title: Sharp Propagation and the Local-to-Nonlocal Transition for Fractional Fisher-KPP Equations on Integer Lattices
summary: Let $P$ denote normalized nearest-neighbor averaging on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and set $A=I-P$. We consider $\partial_tu+A^su=f(u),t>0, x\in\mathbb{Z}^d, 0<s<1.$ For a Fisher-KPP reaction with $a=f'(0)>0$, compactly supported data have logarithmic propagation rate $a/(d+2s)$. In the logistic case, each fixed level set lies between two constant multiples of $\exp(at/(d+2s))$; this localization remains valid for data with the critical algebraic tail. Nondecreasing front-like data in one dimension instead propagate at rate $a/(2s)$, and the resulting acceleration rules out planar traveling fronts of finite speed in every dimension. We also analyze the singular limit $s\uparrow1$. If $τ_s=-\log(1-s)$, then throughout $at<τ_s$ compactly supported solutions follow the Wulff shape of the local nearest-neighbor equation. After a constant multiple of $τ_s$, their propagation is exponential. Half-space data exhibit the corresponding transition from the directional local speed to the exponent $a/(2s)$. The analysis rests on sharp bounds for the subordinated kernel, algebraic barriers, a compactness--Liouville argument, and a decomposition of the fractional walk into its nearest-neighbor and rare long-jump parts.

AI.tldr: This paper studies nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations driven by a fractional power of the discrete Laplacian on Z^d (subordination of nearest-neighbor random walks). For Fisher-KPP reactions, compactly supported data propagate logarithmically at rate a/(d+2s), while front-like data in 1D propagate faster at rate a/(2s) via an acceleration mechanism that rules out planar traveling fronts. In the singular limit s↑1, solutions first follow the Wulff shape of the local equation for times up to τ_s = -log(1-s), then transition to exponential propagation.
AI.motivation: To understand how fractional diffusion (long-range jumps) on lattices alters the propagation dynamics of reaction-diffusion systems compared to the classical local case, particularly regarding propagation speeds, acceleration phenomena, and the singular limit as the fractional exponent approaches 1.
