AI.method: The analysis combines several tools: sharp kernel bounds for the subordinated random walk (fractional Laplacian as a time-changed nearest-neighbor walk), algebraic barrier constructions for upper/lower estimates, a compactness-Liouville argument for characterizing limiting profiles, and a decomposition of the fractional walk into nearest-neighbor and rare long-jump components.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) logarithmic propagation rate a/(d+2s) for compactly supported Fisher-KPP data; (2) exponential-in-time localization of level sets in the logistic case at the same exponent, valid even for critical algebraic tails; (3) faster propagation rate a/(2s) for front-like data in 1D, implying no finite-speed planar fronts in any dimension; (4) in the singular limit s↑1, propagation follows the Wulff shape for at < τ_s, then transitions to exponential growth after roughly τ_s; (5) analogous transition for half-space data from directional local speed to exponential rate a/(2s).
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete picture of propagation regimes for fractional-order discrete reaction-diffusion equations, showing how the balance between short local interactions and rare long jumps—mesured by s—determines whether propagation is logarithmic (for localized data) or exponential (for front-like data), and characterizes the sharp transition as s approaches 1.

title: Frugal Effective Models for Nanophotonic Scattering: Optimizing Global Polarizability Matrices for Metasurface Design
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, supporting information pdf of 11 pages
summary: Accurate nano-photonics simulations of large scale devices like optical metasurfaces require high accuracy reduced models for the device constituents. We present an automated framework for the optimization of Global Polarizability Matrix (GPM) models, which represent a complex scatterer as a small set of non-local effective dipoles. Our goal is to find the most frugal model that reproduces a particle's scattering response within a user-defined accuracy. The method iteratively removes redundant dipoles while re-adapting the positions of the remaining ones via gradient based optimization, stopping at the smallest model that still meets the target. Automatic differentiation, combined with an untrained neural network that reparametrizes the dipole positions, helps to place the dipoles at physically intuitive locations. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach across diverse geometries, from two dimensional ridges over simple spheres to complex three-dimensional particles, achieving compression factors of typically two orders of magnitude compared to full-wave simulations, for target accuracies in the order of few percent. We finally demonstrate how accurate, frugal effective models enable large-scale meta-deflector optimization without periodic approximations. This robust recipe for constructing frugal effective models paves the way for the rapid simulation of large-scale photonic assemblies, required for example for metasurface design.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an automated framework for optimizing Global Polarizability Matrix (GPM) models—representing complex scatterers as small sets of non-local effective dipoles—to create the most frugal reduced models within user-defined accuracy. The method iteratively removes redundant dipoles and re-adapts remaining positions via gradient-based optimization with an untrained neural network reparametrization, achieving ~two orders of magnitude compression versus full-wave simulations and enabling large-scale metasurface optimization without periodic approximations.
AI.motivation: Accurate nano-photonics simulation of large-scale devices like optical metasurfaces requires high-accuracy reduced models for device constituents, since full-wave simulations of such large structures are computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: The framework iteratively removes redundant dipoles from a GPM model while re-adapting the positions of remaining dipoles via gradient-based optimization. Automatic differentiation combined with an untrained neural network reparametrizes dipole positions to place them at physically intuitive locations, stopping when the smallest model meeting the target accuracy is found.
AI.result: Demonstrated versatility across diverse geometries (2D ridges, simple spheres, complex 3D particles), achieving compression factors of approximately two orders of magnitude compared to full-wave simulations with target accuracies of a few percent. The accurate frugal models also enabled large-scale meta-deflector optimization without periodic approximations.
AI.conclusion: The robust automated recipe for constructing frugal effective models enables rapid simulation of large-scale photonic assemblies, paving the way for efficient metasurface design and related photonic applications.

title: A simple shallow neural network for emulating the solution to singularly perturbed problems
summary: We consider (feed-forward) Neural Networks (NNs) for the emulation of the solution to singularly perturbed second order boundary value problems, with two small parameters. We describe a shallow NN which exploits available asymptotic expansions for the solution. These additive decompositions into smooth and layer components, allow for derivative estimates which are explicit in the order of differentiation as well as the singular perturbation parameter(s) \cite{melenk, Irene, SX}. Utilizing such decompositions, we propose a simple NN for emulating the solution to such problems using the $\tanh$ activation function together with different training objectives, such as residual or energy minimization. The key idea is to augment the approximation space with suitable exponential functions, similar to enriched spaces in finite element methods, e.g.~\cite{Kellogg}. Numerical examples in one and two dimensions, including a smooth non-tensor-product domain, illustrate the resulting parameter-robust behavior over the tested perturbation ranges.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes shallow neural networks augmented with exponential basis functions (analogous to enriched spaces in FEM) to emulate solutions of singularly perturbed second-order boundary value problems with two small parameters, leveraging asymptotic decompositions into smooth and layer components.
AI.motivation: Standard neural networks struggle to approximate solutions of singularly perturbed boundary value problems because these solutions contain sharp boundary/interior layers that are difficult to capture, especially when two small perturbation parameters are present.
AI.method: The authors construct a shallow NN using the tanh activation function, enriched with suitable exponential functions in the approximation space (inspired by enriched finite element spaces). They exploit additive asymptotic decompositions of the solution into smooth and layer components, which provide explicit derivative estimates in terms of differentiation order and perturbation parameters. Different training objectives are considered, such as residual or energy minimization.
AI.result: Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions, including a smooth non-tensor-product domain, demonstrate parameter-robust behavior over the tested ranges of perturbation parameters.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting NN approximation spaces with exponentially enriched basis functions, informed by asymptotic analysis, yields robust emulation of singularly perturbed problems with two small parameters.

title: A weighted semigroup approach to exponential stability in linear parabolic equations
summary: This paper establishes the exponential $L^2$-stability of the unique solutions to initial-boundary value problems for linear parabolic partial differential equations with general drift and zero-order coefficients in bounded domains. The key idea lies in constructing a suitable Dirichlet form with respect to a weighted measure $μ= ρ\,dx$ and identifying the corresponding sub-Markovian $C_0$-semigroup of contractions on $L^2(U, μ)$ with the unique weak solution. Remarkably, the exponential $L^2$-stability remains valid even when the zero-order term vanishes, and it holds robustly for all drift coefficients $\mathbf{H} \in L^p(U, \mathbb{R}^d)$ with $p \in (d, \infty)$.

AI.tldr: This paper proves exponential L²-stability for unique solutions to initial-boundary value problems of linear parabolic PDEs with general drift and zero-order coefficients in bounded domains, using Dirichlet forms and sub-Markovian semigroups.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to establish exponential L²-stability for linear parabolic PDEs that holds even when the zero-order term vanishes, and is robust for all drift coefficients in L^p with p > d.
AI.method: The key approach is constructing a Dirichlet form with respect to a weighted measure μ = ρ dx, and identifying the corresponding sub-Markovian C₀-semigroup of contractions on L²(U, μ) with the unique weak solution.
AI.result: Exponential L²-stability is established for the unique weak solutions. This stability remains valid even when the zero-order term vanishes and holds for all drift coefficients H ∈ L^p(U, ℝ^d) with p ∈ (d, ∞).
AI.conclusion: The paper provides robust exponential stability results for a broad class of linear parabolic PDEs under minimal regularity assumptions on the coefficients.

title: Nuclear quantum effects in the thermal conductivity of solid hydrogen
summary: We use a combination of path integral and lattice dynamics methods to calculate the thermal conductivity of solid parahydrogen. Path integral molecular dynamics is first used to calculate a centroid potential of mean force at each temperature, on which a harmonic phonon basis is constructed using the finite displacement method. We then calculate anharmonic force constants on the centroid potential and solve the linearised phonon Boltzmann transport equation for the thermal conductivity. The resulting renormalised phonon dispersion curves, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity are all in remarkably good agreement with experimental measurements. We find that the heat transport is dominated by collective relaxon modes at low temperatures and cannot be captured by making the phonon relaxation time approximation. Indeed, quantitative agreement with the experimental thermal conductivity is only achieved when the nuclear quantum effects in the centroid potential of mean force, phonon boundary scattering, and hydrodynamic transport are all explicitly considered. This is also likely to be the case for other quantum crystals.

AI.tldr: The authors combine path integral molecular dynamics with lattice dynamics to compute the thermal conductivity of solid parahydrogen. They calculate a temperature-dependent centroid potential of mean force, construct harmonic phonons on it, derive anharmonic force constants, and solve the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation. Results for renormalized phonon dispersions, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity agree remarkably well with experiments, but only when nuclear quantum effects, phonon boundary scattering, and hydrodynamic transport are all included. Heat transport at low temperatures is dominated by collective relaxon modes rather than single phonon relaxation.
AI.motivation: Accurately predicting thermal conductivity in quantum crystals like solid parahydrogen is challenging because strong nuclear quantum effects alter the potential energy landscape, and conventional phonon transport approximations (e.g., relaxation time approximation) may fail. The authors aim to develop a method that captures both quantum effects and anharmonic/hydrodynamic transport to achieve quantitative agreement with experiment.
AI.method: Path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) is used to compute a centroid potential of mean force at each temperature. A harmonic phonon basis is constructed on this potential via finite displacement. Anharmonic force constants are then calculated, and the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation is solved to obtain thermal conductivity, including phonon boundary scattering and full hydrodynamic (relaxon) effects.
AI.result: Renormalized phonon dispersion curves, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity all agree remarkably well with experimental measurements. Heat transport at low temperatures is dominated by collective relaxon modes, and quantitative agreement requires explicitly accounting for nuclear quantum effects in the centroid potential, phonon boundary scattering, and hydrodynamic transport.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a path-integral-based renormalized phonon framework can quantitatively capture thermal transport in quantum crystals. It underscores that the relaxation time approximation is insufficient for such materials, since collective/hydrodynamic transport and quantum nuclear effects are essential. The findings likely extend to other quantum crystals.

title: A Generalized Scalar Auxiliary Variable Method for Structure-Preserving and Efficient Integration of Nonlinear port-Hamiltonian DAEs
summary: We develop an energy-optimal generalized scalar auxiliary variable (EOP-GSAV) framework for nonlinear index-one port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations (pH-DAEs). Exploiting the port-Hamiltonian structure, we separate the nonlinear effort, interconnection, and dissipation terms from a constant implicit core. The resulting BDF-1 and BDF-2 schemes require one linear solve per time step with a reusable factorization, while retaining discrete passivity and accurate tracking of the Hamiltonian. The schemes are compared with the implicit midpoint method equipped with full, modified, and frozen-Jacobian Newton iterations. Numerical experiments ranging from a strongly state-dependent nonlinear stress test to large-scale benchmarks demonstrate robust and competitive performance, with substantial efficiency gains in matched-accuracy regimes. A comparison with SUNDIALS IDA shows comparable work-precision behavior at equal order despite a non-specialized Python/SciPy implementation, while unrestricted variable-order adaptive IDA is faster in the high-accuracy regime.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an energy-optimal generalized scalar auxiliary variable (EOP-GSAV) framework for nonlinear index-one port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations (pH-DAEs), producing BDF-1 and BDF-2 schemes that require one linear solve per time step with reusable factorization while retaining discrete passivity and accurate Hamiltonian tracking.
AI.motivation: To address the computational cost and stability challenges in simulating nonlinear port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations, by developing schemes that separate nonlinear efforts from a constant implicit core to enable efficient linear solves while preserving structural properties like passivity and Hamiltonian accuracy.
AI.method: The EOP-GSAV framework exploits the port-Hamiltonian structure to separate nonlinear effort, interconnection, and dissipation terms from a constant implicit core. Two schemes (BDF-1 and BDF-2) are derived, each requiring one linear solve per time step with a reusable factorization. These are benchmarked against implicit midpoint with various Newton iterations and SUNDIALS IDA.
AI.result: Numerical experiments from strongly state-dependent nonlinear stress tests to large-scale benchmarks show robust and competitive performance with substantial efficiency gains in matched-accuracy regimes. Comparison with SUNDIALS IDA shows comparable work-precision at equal order, though unrestricted variable-order adaptive IDA is faster in the high-accuracy regime.
AI.conclusion: The EOP-GSAV BDF-1 and BDF-2 schemes offer an efficient and structure-preserving alternative for solving nonlinear pH-DAEs, competitive with conventional methods in matched-accuracy settings despite a non-specialized Python/SciPy implementation.

title: Global well-posedness of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with helical $L^1$ vorticity
summary: We show that the Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb T$ are globally well posed for initial vorticities that are both helically symmetric and integrable. This class of data typically generates velocity fields of infinite kinetic energy, so this result is not covered by the classical finite-energy well-posedness theory. This result is supercritical from the perspective of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes scaling, and it is made possible by the special structure of helical flows using time-weighted Kato-type spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper proves global well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations on R^2 × T for initial vorticities that are both helically symmetric and integrable, a class that generates infinite kinetic energy velocity fields and is therefore not covered by classical finite-energy theory. The result is supercritical from a 3D Navier-Stokes scaling perspective and is achieved using time-weighted Kato-type spaces that exploit the special structure of helical flows.
AI.motivation: To extend the well-posedness theory of the Navier-Stokes equations beyond the classical finite-energy framework, since helically symmetric data with integrable vorticity naturally produce velocity fields with infinite kinetic energy yet are physically relevant and previously unaddressed by existing theory.
AI.method: The approach leverages the special structure of helical symmetry combined with time-weighted Kato-type spaces to handle the supercritical nature of the problem, enabling a global well-posedness result despite the infinite-energy nature of the velocity fields and the scaling being supercritical in 3D.
AI.result: Global well-posedness is established for Navier-Stokes equations on R^2 × T with helically symmetric and integrable initial vorticities, covering a data class that exceeds the scope of classical finite-energy theory.
AI.conclusion: The helical symmetry of the flows provides enough structural reduction to overcome both the infinite-energy obstruction and the supercritical scaling, yielding a well-posedness result that classical approaches cannot reach.

title: Impact of Data Loss in Postprocessing on Training and Inference of Quantum Neural Networks
summary: As quantum hardware scales to larger devices, the classical software layers that interface with it must evolve in step. Postprocessing routines developed and tested primarily in simulator settings can encode assumptions that no longer hold on utility-scale devices, leading to data loss that can be difficult to detect from high-level model outputs alone. We present a case study of \texttt{SamplerQNN}, the sampling-based quantum neural network class in the Qiskit Machine Learning library. Here, the postprocessing method applies a filter that assumes measurement bit-strings are in virtual qubit space. On our quantum hardware runs, where bit-strings span over 100 physical qubits, this filter led to the loss of 85 to 99.6\% of valid measurement shots, depending on the transpiler's qubit placement. The resulting probability vector is unnormalised, allowing distorted prediction and loss values to propagate through the model without an API-level warning. We demonstrate the impact across five experiments on two IBM backends: for inference, accuracy drops from 0.94 to 0.39 on the same raw measurements; for training, the loss signal is compressed by 22 to 27$\times$, substantially reducing the sensitivity of the optimiser to the objective landscape. The behaviour arises in all released versions of the library (0.8.4 to 0.9.0). We implemented a layout-based marginalisation fix, merged into the GitHub codebase as Pull Request \#1041, that makes \texttt{SamplerQNN} postprocessing forward-compatible with current and upcoming hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study of a critical bug in Qiskit Machine Learning's SamplerQNN, where the postprocessing filter assumes bit-strings are in virtual qubit space, causing 85-99.6% of valid measurement shots to be lost on physical hardware running >100 qubits. This silently corrupts probability vectors, degrading inference accuracy (0.94→0.39) and compressing loss signals 22-27× during training. The issue exists across all library versions (0.8.4-0.9.0) and was fixed via layout-based marginalization in Pull Request #1041.
AI.motivation: As quantum hardware scales to utility-scale devices, postprocessing routines designed and tested in simulator settings can encode faulty assumptions that no longer hold on real hardware, leading to silent data loss that is difficult to detect from high-level model outputs. The authors aim to expose and document this class of problem through a concrete case study.
AI.method: The authors analyze SamplerQNN's postprocessing pipeline in Qiskit Machine Learning, identify the virtual-qubit-space assumption in the bit-string filter, trace its impact across five experiments on two IBM backends with over 100 physical qubits, and implement a layout-based marginalization fix (merged as PR #1041) to make postprocessing forward-compatible.
AI.result: The bug causes 85-99.6% of valid measurement shots to be lost depending on transpiler qubit placement. Inference accuracy drops from 0.94 to 0.39 on identical raw measurements, and training loss signals are compressed by 22-27×, severely reducing optimizer sensitivity. The behavior persists across all released versions (0.8.4-0.9.0) without API-level warning.
AI.conclusion: Simulator-derived postprocessing assumptions can silently corrupt quantum machine learning results on utility-scale hardware. The layout-based marginalization fix addresses the immediate issue and provides a template for ensuring forward compatibility of quantum software layers as hardware scales.

title: Shallow neural network approximation in mixed Sobolev spaces
summary: We investigate the best $L_2$ approximation of mixed Sobolev spaces by shallow neural networks with $n$ neurons and general activation functions. We first establish an activation-independent Fourier-block principle: if an activation has univariate approximation order $ρ$ in the sense of the Fourier-block property, then the global approximation rate has algebraic order $\min\{α,ρ\}$ for target functions of mixed smoothness $α$, up to explicit logarithmic factors. To verify this property for concrete activations, we introduce a structured univariate approximation condition that implies the Fourier-block property with explicit parameters. For $\mathrm{ReLU}^k$, a matching algebraic lower bound identifies $\min\{α,k+1\}$ as the optimal algebraic approximation exponent in any dimension, up to logarithmic factors in the upper bound. The framework also yields the exponent $\min\{α,k+1\}$ for cardinal B-splines and soft-$\mathrm{ReLU}^k$, and the full mixed-smoothness exponent $α$ for ELU and cosine activations, again up to logarithmic~factors.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the optimal L2 approximation rates of mixed Sobolev spaces by shallow neural networks with n neurons and general activation functions, establishing an activation-independent Fourier-block principle and deriving explicit algebraic approximation exponents for various activations (ReLU^k, splines, soft-ReLU^k, ELU, cosine).
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits and capabilities of shallow neural networks in approximating functions with mixed smoothness, and to develop a unified theory that covers general activation functions rather than case-specific analyses.
AI.method: Introduces an activation-independent Fourier-block principle connecting univariate approximation order (ρ) of activations to global mixed-smoothness approximation rates (min{α, ρ} with logarithmic factors). For concrete activations, a structured univariate approximation condition is developed to verify the Fourier-block property with explicit parameters. Matching lower bounds are established for ReLU^k via an algebraic argument.
AI.result: Optimal algebraic approximation exponent is min{α, k+1} for ReLU^k (confirmed by matching lower bound), cardinal B-splines, and soft-ReLU^k in any dimension. Full mixed-smoothness exponent α is achieved for ELU and cosine activations, all up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of optimal approximation rates for shallow networks with general activations on mixed Sobolev spaces, showing that the achievable algebraic order is determined by the minimum of the target smoothness α and the activation's univariate approximation power, with matching lower bounds confirming optimality.

title: Asymptotics for the $k$-Hessian Eigenvalue on the Unit Ball
summary: We compute the limit of the eigenvalue of the $k$-Hessian operator on the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ when $k\rightarrow \infty$, assuming that the ratio $\frac{n}{k}$ remains fixed. When $n< 2ke$, we moreover identify the limit of the corresponding eigenfunctions. We also derive monotonicity results and consider when the ratio varies in $n$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the k-Hessian operator on the unit ball in ℝⁿ as k→∞, with n/k held fixed. The authors compute eigenvalue limits, identify eigenfunction limits when n<2ke, and establish monotonicity results for varying ratios.
AI.motivation: The k-Hessian operator is an important class of nonlinear elliptic operators generalizing the Laplacian (k=1) and the Monge-Ampère operator (k=n). Understanding the asymptotic behavior of its eigenvalues as the parameter k grows large provides insight into the spectrum of these operators and reveals connections to other limiting problems, particularly as the dimension ratio n/k is maintained fixed.
AI.method: The authors compute the limit of eigenvalues of the k-Hessian operator on the unit ball as k→∞ while keeping the ratio n/k fixed. They use analytic techniques to derive the limiting eigenvalue and conditions under which eigenfunction limits can be identified. They also investigate monotonicity properties when the ratio n/k varies with the dimension n.
AI.result: The limiting eigenvalues are computed as k→∞ with n/k fixed. When n<2ke, the corresponding eigenfunction limits are identified. Additionally, monotonicity results are obtained concerning how the eigenvalue behaves when the ratio n/k varies as a function of n.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete asymptotic picture for the eigenvalues of the k-Hessian operator in the large-k regime on the unit ball, including eigenfunction convergence under a specific range condition (n<2ke) and monotonicity properties governing how the ratio n/k affects the spectral behavior.

title: Symmetry-protected triplet Weyl complexes
summary: The Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem dictates that Weyl nodes must appear in pairs of opposite chirality to preserve global charge neutrality. However, in crystals, specific crystalline symmetries can stabilize multi-Weyl nodes, circumventing this pairwise constraint and enabling compensated Weyl complexes with mixed chiral charges. The minimal configuration of this type is a triplet Weyl complex (TWC), comprising exactly three Weyl nodes. Here, we systematically investigate the symmetry conditions required to realize TWCs. By screening all 1651 magnetic space groups (MSGs) in both spinless and spinful systems, we establish that: (i) Only TWCs with charge magnitudes of $\{1,1,2\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$ are permitted; (ii) the $\{1,1,2\}$ configuration can be realized in 166 spinless MSGs and 70 spinful MSGs; and (iii) the $\{1,2,3\}$-TWCs, which has not been reported before, can occur in 10 MSGs for both spinless and spinful cases. We explicitly demonstrate the existence of $\{1,2,3\}$-TWC in a tight-binding model. Furthermore, we present the first electronic realization of $\{1,1,2\}$-TWC topological semimetal state in the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C$_{36}$, in which the three Weyl nodes form a collinear configuration, leading to a characteristic ``S''-shaped surface Fermi arc pattern. Our findings uncover novel topological states featuring mixed chiral charges and provide guidance for exploring their physics in concrete material systems.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically investigates triplet Weyl complexes (TWCs)—groups of exactly three Weyl nodes with mixed chirality that circumvent the Nielsen-Ninomiya pairwise constraint through crystalline symmetries. By screening all 1651 magnetic space groups, the authors establish that only {1,1,2} and {1,2,3} charge configurations are permitted, identify which MSGs can host them, demonstrate a {1,2,3}-TWC in a tight-binding model, and report the first electronic realization of a {1,1,2}-TWC in the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C36.
AI.motivation: The Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem requires Weyl nodes in opposite-chirality pairs, but crystalline symmetries can stabilize multi-Weyl nodes that allow compensated Weyl complexes with mixed chiral charges (TWCs). The authors aim to systematically identify which magnetic space groups can realize these minimal TWC configurations and find real material candidates.
AI.method: The authors screen all 1651 magnetic space groups (MSGs) in both spinless and spinful systems to determine symmetry conditions for TWC realization. They also construct a tight-binding model to explicitly demonstrate a {1,2,3}-TWC and perform first-principles/electronic analysis of the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C36 to realize a {1,1,2}-TWC.
AI.result: Only {1,1,2} and {1,2,3} TWC charge configurations are permitted. The {1,1,2} configuration is possible in 166 spinless and 70 spinful MSGs; the previously unreported {1,2,3} configuration occurs in 10 MSGs for both spinless and spinful cases. A tight-binding model demonstrates the {1,2,3}-TWC, and DZQH-C36 exhibits a {1,1,2}-TWC with collinear Weyl nodes producing a characteristic "S"-shaped surface Fermi arc.
AI.conclusion: The work uncovers new topological states with mixed chiral charges, provides the first comprehensive symmetry classification of TWCs, and offers concrete material guidance for exploring their physics, including a previously unknown {1,2,3} configuration.

title: SparseStack Is an Optimal Oblivious Subspace Embedding
comment: The proof was developed with AI systems
summary: The fully independent SparseStack sketch is a vertical stack of $s$ independent CountSketch matrices, scaled by $s^{-1/2}$, so that every column has exactly $s$ nonzero entries. We prove that it is an oblivious subspace embedding for $d$-dimensional subspaces with distortion $ε$ and failure probability $δ$ when $m = O((d+\log(1/δ))/ε^2)$ and $s = O(\log(d/δ)/ε)$, with explicit constants. These are the parameters conjectured by Nelson and Nguyen (FOCS 2013) for this construction; the row count is optimal by their lower bound. The proof bounds the even moments of the Gram error. A conditional-expectation coupling replaces each signed one-hot column selector by a vector with independent three-point entries, at the cost of a constant factor per moment order. The three-point law has a three-dimensional $L_2$ space, so multiplication by an entry is a $3 \times 3$ Jacobi matrix, and the $2q$-th moment becomes a vacuum matrix element of a deterministic operator on a finite tensor product, graded by total occupation. The operator has three grade bands, and we bound each band on the grade-$ν$ sector by $C(\sqrt{(d+ν+1)/m} + (d+ν+1)/m + (ν+1)/s)$ with $C = 3+\sqrt{2}$. The key step is a shared-factor inequality: each row block of the positive operator attached to one tensor slot is rank one with trace $d$, and the sum over $\ell$ slots sharing the same external factor has norm at most $d+\ell-1$. A $2q$-step expansion and Markov's inequality complete the argument, which is finite-dimensional and does not use Gaussian comparison. The theorem has been formally verified in Lean 4. The proof was developed with AI systems under the author's direction, as disclosed in the paper.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the fully independent SparseStack sketch—a vertical stack of s independent CountSketch matrices scaled by s^{-1/2}—achieves oblivious subspace embedding for d-dimensional subspaces with m = O((d+log(1/δ))/ε²) rows and s = O(log(d/δ)/ε) nonzero entries per column, confirming the parameters conjectured by Nelson and Nguyen. The proof bounds even moments of the Gram error via a conditional-expectation coupling to independent three-point entries, using a ranked-band operator analysis and a shared-factor inequality. The theorem is formally verified in Lean 4.
AI.motivation: The SparseStack sketch is a natural sparse subspace embedding construction conjectured to achieve optimal parameters by Nelson and Nguyen (FOCS 2013), but a rigorous proof of these optimal parameters had been lacking. Proving these bounds settles an open conjecture and provides tight guarantees for a practically relevant sparse embedding.
AI.method: The proof bounds the even moments of the Gram error. A conditional-expectation coupling replaces each signed one-hot column selector with a vector of independent three-point entries, costing only a constant factor per moment order. The three-point law yields a 3-dimensional L2 space, so entry multiplication becomes a 3×3 Jacobi matrix, and the 2q-th moment becomes a vacuum matrix element of a deterministic graded operator on a finite tensor product. The operator has three grade bands, each bounded on the grade-ν sector by C(√((d+ν+1)/m) + (d+ν+1)/m + (ν+1)/s) with C = 3+√2. A key shared-factor inequality shows rank-one row blocks with trace d, and the sum over ℓ slots sharing an external factor has norm at most d+ℓ−1. A 2q-step expansion and Markov's inequality complete the argument. The proof is finite-dimensional and avoids Gaussian comparison.
AI.result: The paper proves that SparseStack achieves oblivious subspace embedding with m = O((d+log(1/δ))/ε²) rows and s = O(log(d/δ)/ε) sparsity per column with explicit constants, matching the Nelson–Nguyen conjecture. The row count matches the known lower bound, making it optimal. The theorem has been formally verified in Lean 4.
AI.conclusion: This work settles an open conjecture by providing a rigorous proof of optimal oblivious subspace embedding parameters for the SparseStack sketch. The proof technique—using moment bounds, operator methods on tensor products, and a novel shared-factor inequality—may be broadly applicable to other sparse sketching constructions. The Lean 4 formal verification adds strong confidence in the correctness of the argument.

title: Asymptotic expansion of the voltage potential under small Robin perturbations of its boundary conditions
summary: Inspired by questions related to inverse problems and shape optimization, we derive an asymptotic expansion of the voltage potential, solution to a model elliptic second-order partial differential equation, under small perturbations of its boundary conditions. More precisely, the homogeneous Dirichlet or homogeneous Neumann boundary condition in a fixed, reference configuration of the problem is replaced by a Robin boundary condition with admittance $k_\varepsilon > 0$ on a ``small'' subset $ω_\varepsilon$ of the boundary of the ambient domain, vanishing at the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$. In each of these two situations, a general asymptotic formula is established for the voltage potential, which rests on minimal assumptions about the shape of the vanishing subset $ω_\varepsilon$ and the parameter $k_\varepsilon$. The scalings of these expansions, capturing the intensity of the perturbation, are measured by new quantities called ``Robin-Dirichlet'' capacity or a ``Robin-Neumann'' capacity, which depend on the geometry of $ω_\varepsilon$ and on the value of the parameter $k_\varepsilon$. We analyze how these quantities compare to more classical measures of the ``smallness'' of $ω_\varepsilon$, such as the capacity or the Neumann capacity of $ω_\varepsilon$, according to the behavior of $k_\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.

AI.tldr: The paper derives asymptotic expansions of the voltage potential (solution to an elliptic PDE) when homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions are replaced by Robin boundary conditions on a small subset of the boundary that vanishes in the limit. The expansions introduce new "Robin-Dirichlet" and "Robin-Neumann" capacities that quantify the perturbation's intensity, and the paper compares these to classical capacity measures.
AI.motivation: Motivated by inverse problems and shape optimization, the authors seek to understand how small perturbations of boundary conditions (switching from Dirichlet/Neumann to Robin on a tiny boundary subset) affect the solution to an elliptic PDE, generalizing earlier results to broader settings.
AI.method: The authors derive a general asymptotic formula for the voltage potential under minimal assumptions on the geometry of the small subset ω_ε and the Robin admittance parameter k_ε. They introduce new quantities—Robin-Dirichlet and Robin-Neumann capacities—to measure the scaling/strength of the expansion, and then analyze how these capacities relate to classical capacities (standard or Neumann capacity) depending on the asymptotic behavior of k_ε.
AI.result: A general asymptotic expansion is established for both the Dirichlet-to-Robin and Neumann-to-Robin perturbation scenarios. New capacity notions are defined and systematically compared to classical smallness measures of the perturbed subset, with their relative ordering depending on the rate at which k_ε decays as ε → 0.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a unified and mathematically rigorous framework for analyzing boundary condition perturbations in elliptic problems, introducing novel capacities that naturally capture the perturbation's effect and connecting them to existing capacity theory.

title: An Aeroelastic Solver Integrating Reformulated-Vortex-Particle and Finite-Element Methods across Non-Conforming Interfaces
comment: Preprint to be submitted to Elsevier
summary: We present $\texttt{VarFlExI}$ (Variable Fidelity Unsteady Flow-FEniCS Exchange Interface), a modular aeroelastic solver for modeling two-way fluid-structure interaction (FSI) of flexible lifting surfaces. The framework employs a reformulated Vortex Particle Method (rVPM) to solve the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations without the need for computationally expensive volumetric meshing, while supporting variable-fidelity aerodynamic modeling using the $\texttt{FLOWUnsteady}$ framework. On the structural side, a Reissner-Mindlin plate formulation is discretized using the finite element method and integrated in time through the generalized-$α$ method, with the nonlinear equilibrium equations solved using a Gauss-Newton procedure within the $\texttt{FEniCS}$ framework. Fluid and structural solvers are coupled through an explicit staggered partitioned scheme, ensuring conservation of virtual work for load and displacement transfer across the non-matching interface. To accommodate the multi-representative nature of the aerodynamic loads and geometry, the interface coupling employs separate work-conservative force and reverse-geometry transfer operators via a common intermediate interface. The framework is validated against water-tunnel experiments, demonstrating accurate prediction of the coupled aeroelastic response rather than independent validation of the constituent solvers. The computational efficiency of the meshless aerodynamic solver enables simulations at significantly lower computational cost while maintaining accuracy. The solver is further evaluated through sensitivity analyses and parameter studies spanning different flow conditions, structural properties, and coupling parameters.

AI.tldr: VarFlExI is a modular aeroelastic solver for two-way fluid-structure interaction of flexible lifting surfaces, combining a reformulated Vortex Particle Method (rVPM) with a Reissner-Mindlin plate finite element formulation. It uses an explicit staggered partitioned coupling scheme with work-conservative force and reverse-geometry transfer operators, and is validated against water-tunnel experiments showing accurate aeroelastic prediction at significantly lower computational cost than volumetric mesh-based approaches.
AI.motivation: To model two-way fluid-structure interaction of flexible lifting surfaces accurately and efficiently, avoiding the high computational cost associated with volumetric meshing while enabling variable-fidelity aerodynamic analysis within a modular framework.
AI.method: Uses a reformulated Vortex Particle Method (rVPM) for meshless incompressible Navier-Stokes solutions, integrated with FLOWUnsteady for variable-fidelity aerodynamics. The structural side employs a Reissner-Mindlin plate finite element discretization with generalized-alpha time integration and Gauss-Newton nonlinear solving within FEniCS. Fluid-structure coupling uses an explicit staggered partitioned scheme with separate work-conservative force and reverse-geometry transfer operators through a common intermediate interface.
AI.result: Validated against water-tunnel experiments, demonstrating accurate prediction of coupled aeroelastic response. The meshless aerodynamic solver achieves significant computational cost reduction while maintaining accuracy. Sensitivity analyses and parameter studies across flow conditions, structural properties, and coupling parameters further evaluate the framework.
AI.conclusion: VarFlExI provides a computationally efficient and accurate modular framework for aeroelastic simulation of flexible lifting surfaces, validated at the coupled system level rather than through independent solver validation.

title: Computing Lewis Weights to High Precision by Fixed-Point Iteration
summary:
The $\ell_p$-Lewis weights of a matrix are defined by a fixed-point equation. For $p<4$, Cohen and Peng [CP15] showed that iterating an equivalent rearrangement of this equation computes Lewis weights to high precision; for $p\geq4$, prior high-precision methods instead use optimization-based approaches. We show that the direct Lewis fixed-point iteration, appearing in the thesis of Lee [Lee16], computes Lewis weights to high precision for every $p>2$.
  For a matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ partitioned into row blocks $\mathbf{A}_{[1]},\ldots,\mathbf{A}_{[k]}$, we compute, for $p>2$, coordinatewise $\varepsilon$-approximate $\ell_p$ block Lewis weights in $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}_{[i]})}}{\varepsilon}\right)$ rounds of exact leverage-score-vector computations. For ordinary Lewis weights, this becomes $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{m}}{\varepsilon}\right)$, improving the $O\left(p^2\log(m/\varepsilon)\right)$ bound of Gribling, Sidford, and Zhang [GSZ26] for $p\geq4$.
  Our main observation is that each direct Lewis update contracts the KL divergence to the true weights by a factor of $1-\frac{2}{p}$. We also give an alternate explanation of this contraction through volume sampling and entropic independence. Synthetic experiments closely match our predicted local contraction rates and iteration counts grow approximately linearly with $p$; real-data experiments illustrate the information-concentration tradeoff of finite-$p$ block Lewis designs.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that direct Lewis fixed-point iteration computes ℓ_p Lewis weights to high precision for all p > 2, improving prior results that only covered p < 4 or required optimization-based approaches. It achieves coordinatewise ε-approximate block Lewis weights in O(p log(p√Σrank/ε)) rounds of exact leverage-score computations, and establishes the key contraction of KL divergence by factor (1-2/p) per iteration.
AI.motivation: Lewis weights are important for sampling and dimension reduction in p-norms, but prior algorithmic guarantees for computing them at high precision were limited: fixed-point iteration was only proven for p < 4, while p ≥ 4 required optimization-based approaches with worse bounds. The direct fixed-point iteration suggested by Lee's thesis was conjectured to work but lacked rigorous guarantees. A deeper understanding of its convergence would yield simpler and faster algorithms across all p > 2.
AI.method: The authors analyze the direct Lewis fixed-point iteration scheme and show that each update contracts the KL divergence between the current iterate and the true Lewis weights by a multiplicative factor of (1 - 2/p). They leverage this contraction to bound the number of iterations needed for high-precision computation. They also provide an alternative explanation of the contraction via volume sampling and entropic independence, and validate their theory with synthetic and real-data experiments.
AI.result: For a matrix A with row blocks A_[1],...,A_[k], the method computes coordinatewise ε-approximate ℓ_p block Lewis weights for p > 2 in O(p log(p√Σ rank(A_[i])/ε)) rounds of exact leverage-score-vector computations. For ordinary Lewis weights this becomes O(p log(p√m/ε)), improving the O(p² log(m/ε)) bound of Gribling, Sidford, and Zhang for p ≥ 4. Synthetic experiments match predicted local contraction rates with iteration counts growing approximately linearly in p.
AI.conclusion: The direct Lewis fixed-point iteration is a provably efficient algorithm for computing Lewis weights at high precision for all p > 2, not just p < 4 as previously known. The KL-divergence contraction argument provides a clean theoretical basis, and the empirical results support the theory while illustrating practical tradeoffs for finite-p block Lewis designs on real data.

title: Solutions to fourth order degenerate parabolic equations obtained via weighted energy dissipation
summary: We apply the variational method of Weighted Energy Dissipation (WED) to obtain a global-in-time approximation of solutions to fourth order degenerate parabolic equations of Cahn-Hilliard type. Differently from the standard approach to the existence theory, WED induces an elliptic regularization in time, not in space. The confinement on the phase field is guaranteed already for the approximation, a priori estimates follow without modification of Lyapunov functionals, and the approximations are weakly differentiable in time --- even twice in the case of linear mobility. While WED has been widely used for the construction of gradient flows in Hilbert spaces, this appears to be the first application of WED to a metric gradient flow beyond second order PDEs of Wasserstein type.

AI.tldr: The authors apply the Weighted Energy Dissipation (WED) variational method to approximate solutions of fourth-order degenerate parabolic Cahn-Hilliard-type equations globally in time, marking the first application of WED to a metric gradient flow beyond second-order Wasserstein-type PDEs.
AI.motivation: To extend the applicability of the WED variational method to higher-order degenerate parabolic equations of Cahn-Hilliard type, and to demonstrate that WED provides advantages over standard existence theory approaches — including direct phase-field confinement, simpler a priori estimates without Lyapunov functional modifications, and improved time regularity of approximations.
AI.method: The paper uses the Weighted Energy Dissipation (WED) variational approach, which induces an elliptic regularization in time (rather than in space as in standard approaches). The method is applied to fourth-order degenerate parabolic Cahn-Hilliard-type equations treated as metric gradient flows. Approximations remain confined in the phase field, require no functional modification for a priori estimates, and are weakly differentiable in time — twice differentiable in the case of linear mobility.
AI.result: The WED method successfully yields global-in-time approximations to solutions of fourth-order degenerate Cahn-Hilliard-type equations, with the phase-field confinement preserved already at the approximation level and appropriate regularity properties of the approximants established (weak time differentiability, and twice differentiability for linear mobility case).
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that WED can be effectively employed for metric gradient flows beyond second-order Wasserstein-type PDEs, establishing a novel connection between variational approximation methods and higher-order degenerate parabolic equations of Cahn-Hilliard type.

title: Existence of thermodynamically consistent solutions for data-driven porous media problems
summary: Data-Driven Computational Mechanics (DDCM) replaces traditional phenomenological constitutive models by directly reformulating boundary-value problems in terms of local material state data obtained from experiments or fine-scale simulations. Standard DDCM formulations, only enforcing equilibrium and compatibility, do not inherently guarantee compliance with the second law of thermodynamics. This breakdown occurs particularly when input material data sets are subject to noise or local physical non-admissibility. In this work, we present a variational DDCM framework specifically tailored to diffusion--reaction problems. Taking advantage of the simplicity of the thermodynamic constraint in gradient-flux systems, we propose an augmented formulation that explicitly enforces the second law of thermodynamics as a hard constraint within the energy-minimization problem. Although the set of thermodynamically admissible states is non-convex and fails to be weakly closed in the ambient phase space, we establish existence of minimizers by proving that the intersection of the admissible set with the subspace of fields that are compatible and in equilibrium is weakly sequentially closed via a compensated compactness argument. To enable practical computations, we analyze both a Lagrange multiplier formulation and a penalization scheme. We prove the $Γ$-convergence of the penalized functionals to the exact constrained problem and establish a fully discrete convergence framework incorporating spatial finite-element discretization and empirical data-set approximations. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed penalty scheme effectively restores thermodynamic consistency even in the presence of severely corrupted material data.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a variational Data-Driven Computational Mechanics (DDCM) framework for diffusion-reaction problems that explicitly enforces the second law of thermodynamics as a hard constraint within the energy-minimization formulation. The authors prove existence of minimizers via compensated compactness, analyze Lagrange multiplier and penalization schemes, establish Γ-convergence and a fully discrete convergence framework, and demonstrate through numerical experiments that the penalty scheme restores thermodynamic consistency even with corrupted material data.
AI.motivation: Standard DDCM formulations enforce only equilibrium and compatibility constraints, which do not inherently guarantee compliance with the second law of thermodynamics—especially when input material data sets are noisy or physically non-admissible. This can lead to physically meaningless solutions, motivating the need for a framework that explicitly enforces thermodynamic admissibility.
AI.method: The authors develop a variational DDCM framework for diffusion-reaction problems by leveraging the simplicity of thermodynamic constraints in gradient-flux systems. They augment the energy-minimization formulation to enforce the second law as a hard constraint, use a compensated compactness argument to establish existence of minimizers despite the non-convex admissible set, and analyze both a Lagrange multiplier formulation and a penalization scheme. They prove Γ-convergence of penalized functionals and establish a fully discrete convergence framework with finite-element discretization and empirical data approximations.
AI.result: The paper establishes rigorous mathematical foundations (existence of minimizers via compensated compactness, Γ-convergence of penalized functionals, fully discrete convergence) and confirms through numerical experiments that the proposed penalty scheme effectively restores thermodynamic consistency, even when material data is severely corrupted.
AI.conclusion: The augmented variational DDCM framework successfully enforces thermodynamic admissibility as a hard constraint in diffusion-reaction problems, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical, convergent numerical schemes that maintain physical consistency even under noisy or non-admissible data conditions.

title: Numerical experiments on the Hardy conjecture for the Gauss circle problem
summary: The classical unsolved Gauss circle problem concerns estimating the error between the number of lattice points inside a circle and the area of the circle as its radius tends to infinity. About a century ago, Hardy proposed a conjecture concerning this problem. In this paper, we attempt to provide numerical evidence in support of the Hardy conjecture through large-scale numerical computations.

AI.tldr: This paper provides large-scale numerical evidence supporting the Hardy conjecture related to the classical unsolved Gauss circle problem, which estimates the error between lattice point counts inside a circle and the circle's area.
AI.motivation: The Gauss circle problem is a classical unsolved problem in number theory, and Hardy proposed a conjecture about it roughly a century ago. The authors aim to provide numerical evidence supporting this conjecture, which has remained unproven.
AI.method: The authors perform large-scale numerical computations to gather evidence in support of the Hardy conjecture concerning the error estimation in the Gauss circle problem.
AI.result: The paper presents numerical evidence that appears to support the Hardy conjecture based on large-scale computations.
AI.conclusion: The numerical findings support the Hardy conjecture for the Gauss circle problem, though formal proof remains open.

title: Harmonic morphisms of sub-Riemannian Lie groups
summary: We prove that harmonic morphisms between sub-Riemannian Lie groups are smooth, are symmetries of the sub-Riemannian Laplacian and are conformal submersions that satisfy a particular PDE. Moreover, we give some partial results for harmonic morphisms beyond Lie groups. We show the existence of harmonic coordinates for harmonically homogeneous spaces, and that smooth harmonic morphisms are symmetries of the Laplacian in all sub-Riemannian manifolds. Finally, we compute the first variation of the horizontal energy along a harmonic morphism of sub-Riemannian Lie groups: it is given by a linear form on the Lie algebra of the target, the modular mismatch, which vanishes for Riemannian and Carnot targets, but surprisingly not in general. Therefore, unlike in the Riemannian case, harmonic morphisms of sub-Riemannian Lie groups need not be harmonic maps.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that harmonic morphisms between sub-Riemannian Lie groups are smooth, serve as symmetries of the sub-Riemannian Laplacian, and are conformal submersions satisfying a specific PDE. It also shows the existence of harmonic coordinates for harmonically homogeneous spaces, establishes that smooth harmonic morphisms are Laplacian symmetries in all sub-Riemannian manifolds, and computes the first variation of horizontal energy along such morphisms—revealing a "modular mismatch" term that vanishes for Riemannian and Carnot targets but not in general, meaning harmonic morphisms of sub-Riemannian Lie groups need not be harmonic maps, unlike in Riemannian geometry.
AI.motivation: To extend the theory of harmonic morphisms—map preserving harmonic functions—from Riemannian to sub-Riemannian settings, particularly on Lie groups, where smoothness, PDE characterizations, and relationships to harmonic maps were previously unclear.
AI.method: The paper uses analytic and geometric arguments to establish regularity (smoothness) results, derives structural characterizations (conformal submersions satisfying a PDE), and computes variational formulas (first variation of horizontal energy) to identify when harmonic morphisms coincide with harmonic maps via a "modular mismatch" term.
AI.result: Harmonic morphisms between sub-Riemannian Lie groups are smooth, conformal submersions, and Laplacian symmetries. Harmonic coordinates exist for harmonically homogeneous spaces, and smooth harmonic morphisms are Laplacian symmetries generally. The first variation of horizontal energy introduces a modular mismatch—zero for Riemannian and Carnot targets but generally nonzero—so harmonic morphisms need not be harmonic maps in sub-Riemannian Lie groups.
AI.conclusion: Harmonic morphisms in the sub-Riemannian Lie group setting largely parallel the Riemannian theory but diverge in an important way: they are not necessarily harmonic maps due to the modular mismatch, revealing a marked structural difference between Riemannian and non-Riemannian (non-Carnot) sub-Riemannian geometries.

title: Fast Gauss Sums via Flash Attention
summary: Gaussian kernel sums are the computational core of maximum mean discrepancies (MMDs), kernel gradient flows, Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD), and many other kernel methods. At the same time, softmax attention has received an extraordinary amount of hardware-aware code engineering, culminating in flash attention. We show that Gauss kernel sums with arbitrary, signed weights can be evaluated via flash attention: two small input augmentations turn the normalized softmax reduction into the unnormalized Gauss sum, without writing a single line of custom GPU code. For feature dimension D>8 in fp16, this approach beats compiled PyTorch code as well as PyKeOps kernels (often significantly) in speed, memory-overhead and accuracy. Indeed, its memory scaling remains linear.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Gaussian kernel sums with arbitrary signed weights can be evaluated via flash attention through two simple input augmentations, leveraging the highly optimized softmax attention implementation without needing custom GPU code, outperforming PyTorch and PyKeOps for D>8 in fp16.
AI.motivation: Gaussian kernel sums are fundamental to many kernel methods (MMD, kernel gradient flows, SVGD), yet they lack the hardware-aware optimization that softmax attention has received through extensive engineering like flash attention. The goal is to bridge this gap by exploiting existing optimized attention implementations.
AI.method: Two small input augmentations transform the normalized softmax reduction into an unnormalized Gauss sum, allowing Gaussian kernel sums with arbitrary signed weights to be computed through flash attention without writing custom GPU code.
AI.result: For feature dimension D>8 in fp16, this flash attention-based approach beats compiled PyTorch code and PyKeOps kernels, often significantly, in terms of speed, memory overhead, and accuracy, while maintaining linear memory scaling.
AI.conclusion: Flash attention can be repurposed as a highly efficient backend for Gaussian kernel sums, achieving superior performance by leveraging existing hardware-aware engineering for attention mechanisms.

title: On the Abundance of Critical Points of the t-SNE Energy
summary: This paper considers the energy landscape of the t-SNE algorithm. While this algorithm has enjoyed broad adoption, the non-convexity of the associated energy has made it difficult to rigorously understand what the algorithm captures in many settings. In particular, a number of well-known numerical examples, several of which are reproduced in this article, suggest a complicated energy landscape with many local minimizers that do not respect the topology or clustering structure of the underlying data. This work seeks to provide first steps towards a rigorous explanation of these phenomena. Specifically, for a general family of energies, which include both the original t-SNE algorithm and recently identified large data limits, and for densities in feature space which obey a continuous symmetry, we construct infinite families of distinct critical points. These critical points are based upon identifying pairs of discrete symmetries, one in the original feature space and the other in the target embedding space, which are preserved under gradient dynamics. These critical configurations exhibit many characteristics, such as topology breaking and spurious clustering, which are often observed empirically. Finally, numerical and analytical examples are given throughout as a means of illustrating the approach.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis of the t-SNE energy landscape, constructing infinite families of distinct critical points that arise from pairings of discrete symmetries in feature and embedding spaces, thereby explaining empirically observed phenomena like topology breaking and spurious clustering.
AI.motivation: t-SNE is widely used but its non-convex energy landscape is poorly understood. Numerous numerical examples show complicated energy landscapes with many local minimizers that fail to respect the topology or clustering structure of the underlying data. The authors seek to provide rigorous first steps toward explaining these phenomena.
AI.method: For a general family of energies (including original t-SNE and large data limits) and densities in feature space with continuous symmetry, the authors construct infinite families of distinct critical points by identifying pairs of discrete symmetries—one in feature space and one in target embedding space—that are preserved under gradient dynamics.
AI.result: The constructed critical configurations exhibit characteristics such as topology breaking and spurious clustering, which are often observed empirically. Numerical and analytical examples are provided throughout to illustrate the approach.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a rigorous explanation for the intricate energy landscape of t-SNE, showing that topology-breaking and spurious clustering phenomena arise from symmetry-induced critical points, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding these well-known empirical observations.

title: A Bernstein problem for translating solutions to the mean curvature flow
summary:
We study entire graphical translating solutions of the mean curvature flow, \[ \operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{\nabla G}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla G|^2}}\right)
  =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla G|^2}}
  \qquad\text{in }\mathbb R^N. \] Every such graph is mean-convex, since its mean curvature is the vertical component of its unit normal. In dimension two, mean-convex translating solitons are convex, and an entire graphical translator is therefore the rotationally symmetric bowl soliton. In higher dimensions Wang constructed non-rotational entire convex translating graphs. We prove that a further loss of rigidity occurs at the Bernstein dimension: for every $N\ge 8$ there exists a one-parameter family of entire graphical translators that are mean-convex but not convex.
  The construction starts from the Bombieri--De Giorgi--Giusti (BDG) entire minimal graph in $\mathbb R^8$ and develops a singular perturbation theory for the translator equation around it. The main new feature is a transition layer near Simons' cone: the translating term breaks the odd symmetry of the minimal graph, and after a suitable recentering the matching problem is governed by a parabolic inner equation. A detailed analysis of this layer, together with weighted Jacobi theory on the BDG graph and global barriers, yields the desired entire solutions.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs entire graphical translating solutions of mean curvature flow in dimensions N≥8 that are mean-convex but not convex, breaking rigidity known in lower dimensions. Starting from the Bombieri–De Giorgi–Giusti entire minimal graph in R^8, a singular perturbation analysis yields a one-parameter family of non-convex translators via a transition layer near Simons' cone.
AI.motivation: In dimension two, mean-convex translating solitons are necessarily convex, making the rotationally symmetric bowl soliton the only entire graphical translator. In higher dimensions Wang found non-rotational convex examples, but the question of whether mean-convexity alone still forces convexity remained open. This paper shows rigidity is lost entirely at the Bernstein dimension N=8.
AI.method: The construction uses singular perturbation theory around the BDG entire minimal graph in R^8. Key ingredients include: (1) a transition layer analysis near Simons' cone since the translating term breaks the odd symmetry of the minimal graph; (2) a parabolic inner equation governing the matching problem after recentering; (3) weighted Jacobi theory on the BDG graph; and (4) global barriers to control the full solution.
AI.result: For every N≥8, there exists a one-parameter family of entire graphical translators of mean curvature flow that are mean-convex but not convex.
AI.conclusion: The rigidity of two-dimensional mean-convex translators (convexity implying bowl soliton) completely fails starting at dimension N=8, where non-convex mean-convex entire translators exist in abundance. This marks the Bernstein dimension as a sharp threshold for a new class of solutions.

title: PRICE: A Systematic Study of LLM Adaptation Choices for Bitcoin Price Forecasting
summary: Cryptocurrency markets exhibit extreme volatility and non-stationary dynamics that challenge conventional forecasting methods. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for time series forecasting, the combined effects of adaptation choices remain largely unexplored in financial settings. This study introduces PRICE, a structured approach for adapting LLMs to short-term Bitcoin price forecasting. Built on a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B model, PRICE investigates how fine-tuning, numerical representation, prompting, inference, and decoding jointly influence forecasting performance. PRICE integrates Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Recursive multi-step inference, Integer-rounded numerical representation, Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompting, and Exact zero-temperature decoding. Ablation studies show that each component contributes to forecasting accuracy and reliability. LoRA enables efficient training on limited hardware, recursive inference improves accuracy, integer-rounded values reduce errors, CTF prompting outperforms Chain-of-Thought, Implicit Chain-of-Thought (iCoT), and few-shot prompting, and zero-temperature decoding improves stability during recursive forecasting. Comparative evaluation against eight transformer-based and time-series foundation models shows that PRICE achieves the lowest forecasting errors on both validation and test sets while maintaining robust performance across evaluation periods. Despite being based on a model primarily pretrained on text rather than time-series data, PRICE achieves competitive or superior performance relative to specialized foundation models. These findings demonstrate that adaptation choices critically determine the accuracy and robustness of LLMs for numerical time-series forecasting.

AI.tldr: PRICE is a structured approach for adapting LLMs (built on a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B) to short-term Bitcoin price forecasting, combining LoRA fine-tuning, recursive multi-step inference, integer-rounded numerical representation, Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompting, and exact zero-temperature decoding. It outperforms eight transformer-based and time-series foundation models on forecasting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Cryptocurrency markets are highly volatile and non-stationary, making forecasting difficult. While LLMs show promise for time series forecasting, the combined effects of different adaptation choices (fine-tuning, prompting, inference, decoding, numerical representation) in financial settings remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: PRICE integrates five key components: (1) Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for efficient training on limited hardware, (2) Recursive multi-step inference for improved accuracy, (3) Integer-rounded numerical representation to reduce errors, (4) Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompting which outperforms Chain-of-Thought, Implicit Chain-of-Thought, and few-shot prompting, and (5) Exact zero-temperature decoding for stability during recursive forecasting. Ablation studies isolate the contribution of each component.
AI.result: Ablation studies confirm each component contributes to forecasting accuracy and reliability. Comparative evaluation against eight transformer-based and time-series foundation models shows PRICE achieves the lowest forecasting errors on both validation and test sets, with robust performance across evaluation periods. PRICE achieves competitive or superior performance relative to specialized foundation models despite being based on a text-pretrained model.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation choices critically determine the accuracy and robustness of LLMs for numerical time-series forecasting. The structured combination of fine-tuning strategy, prompting technique, numerical representation, inference mode, and decoding settings can make text-pretrained LLMs competitive with or superior to specialized time-series foundation models in volatile financial domains.

title: Naked Singularities beyond Spherical Symmetry: Instability of $κ$-Self-Similar Solutions via an Iteration Scheme
summary: This paper provides the instability counterpart to our recent construction of nonspherically symmetric approximating $κ$-self-similar naked-singularity solutions for the Einstein--scalar field system. These singular solutions contain pervasive nonspherical borderline terms, and to prove instability the delicate renormalization procedure developed in [2] does not extend to the more singular setting considered here. To overcome these difficulties, we introduce a new iteration scheme adapted to singular backgrounds whose leading-order geometry depends on the angular variables. At each step, the nonlinear coefficients are frozen using the preceding double-null geometry, and the resulting equations are solved in a triangular order. In this way, the nonspherical borderline terms are incorporated into the approximate geometry rather than treated as perturbative errors, yielding successively sharper estimates. After sufficiently many iterations, the scheme controls the singular angular structure and produces an approximate spacetime whose difference from the exact solution satisfies the required bounds. In particular, these bounds provide an existence region large enough to carry out the instability argument. We further prove that anisotropic perturbations of the outgoing data, arbitrarily small in a scale-critical norm, lead to the formation of a trapped surface. We also formulate and verify a matter-focusing condition under which a parabolic flow argument guarantees the existence of a corresponding marginally outer trapped surface (MOTS). Together, these results establish the nonlinear instability of $κ$-self-similar naked singularities beyond spherical symmetry in the Einstein--scalar field system and introduce a framework for applications across Einstein systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the nonlinear instability of nonspherically symmetric κ-self-similar naked-singularity solutions in the Einstein-scalar field system, introducing a new iteration scheme adapted to singular backgrounds with angular-dependent leading-order geometry. The scheme freezes nonlinear coefficients using the preceding double-null geometry and solves equations in triangular order, incorporating nonspherical borderline terms into the approximate geometry. Results show trapped surface formation from arbitrarily small anisotropic perturbations and establish a MOTS via a matter-focusing condition.
AI.motivation: The work addresses the instability counterpart to prior constructions of nonspherically symmetric approximating κ-self-similar naked-singularity solutions for the Einstein-scalar field system. The singular solutions contain pervasive nonspherical borderline terms, and existing renormalization procedures do not extend to this more singular setting, necessitating a fundamentally new approach.
AI.method: A novel iteration scheme is introduced for singular backgrounds whose leading-order geometry depends on angular variables. At each step, nonlinear coefficients are frozen using the preceding double-null geometry, and equations are solved in triangular order. Nonspherical borderline terms are incorporated directly into the approximate geometry rather than treated as perturbative errors, yielding successively sharper estimates. A parabolic flow argument under a matter-focusing condition is used to guarantee MOTS existence.
AI.result: After sufficient iterations, the scheme controls the singular angular structure and produces an approximate spacetime whose difference from the exact solution satisfies required bounds, providing an existence region large enough for the instability argument. Anisotropic perturbations of outgoing data, arbitrarily small in a scale-critical norm, lead to trapped surface formation. A matter-focusing condition is formulated and verified under which a MOTS exists.
AI.conclusion: The results establish nonlinear instability of κ-self-similar naked singularities beyond spherical symmetry in the Einstein-scalar field system, and introduce a broadly applicable framework for instability analysis across Einstein systems.

title: From plans to maps: Nonlocal regularization of optimal transport
summary: We introduce a nonlocal regularization of optimal transport that bridges Kantorovich and Monge formulations. The regularization penalizes oscillations through an interaction kernel singular near the diagonal. We show that, for sufficiently strong singularities, every finite-energy transport plan is induced by a map, yielding equivalence between the regularized Kantorovich and Monge problems. For fractional kernels, the regularizer reduces to a fractional Sobolev seminorm that can allow jump discontinuities, leading to existence results for broad classes of source and target measures. We derive first-order optimality conditions and analyze the vanishing-regularization limit. The regularized functionals $Γ$-converge to the classical Kantorovich problem, while the first-order $Γ$-limit selects, whenever they exist, finite-energy Monge minimizers with minimal nonlocal energy. When no such minimizer exists, we identify a different asymptotic regime and establish a sharp scaling law in a prototypical mass-splitting example. Finally, after lifting the problem to the product of transport plans, we derive a dual formulation using the cone of copositive functions and propose a fixed-point numerical scheme illustrating the regularization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a nonlocal regularization of optimal transport that bridges Kantorovich and Monge formulations, penalizing oscillations via singular interaction kernels. For sufficiently strong singularities, finite-energy transport plans are induced by maps, making the regularized problems equivalent. The paper analyzes convergence behavior, derives optimality conditions, establishes Γ-convergence results to classical and Monge-minimizer limits, identifies scaling laws in mass-splitting cases, and proposes a dual formulation with a fixed-point numerical scheme.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between the Kantorovich and Monge formulations of optimal transport by introducing a regularization that can enforce Monge-type (map-induced) solutions within the more flexible Kantorovich framework, while handling broad classes of measures including those with discontinuities.
AI.method: Introduces a nonlocal energy term with singular interaction kernels near the diagonal to penalize oscillations. Uses fractional Sobolev seminorms for fractional kernels, derives first-order optimality conditions, performs Γ-convergence analysis of the vanishing-regularization limit, lifts to product space for dual formulation using copositive functions, and proposes a fixed-point numerical scheme.
AI.result: Shows that strong singularities force finite-energy transport plans to be map-induced (Kantorovich-Monge equivalence). title: Higher Order Unbounded Rough Drivers
summary: We construct a framework for higher order unbounded rough drivers defined by rough paths over vector fields. This allows us to consider a purely Eulerian perspective for rough transport equations where the driving rough path vector field is allowed to have temporal $\mathfrak{p}$-variation for any $\mathfrak{p} \in (1,\infty)$. We use this framework to show the well-posedness of an equation with two transport terms; one driven by a rough path vector field with aforementioned $\mathfrak{p}$-variation in time, and the other driven by a DiPerna--Lions-type drift vector field.

The framework is used to prove well-posedness of transport equations combining two transport terms: one driven by a rough path vector field with this p-variation and another driven by a DiPerna–Lions-type drift field.
AI.motivation: To extend rough transport equation theory to a purely Eulerian setting where the temporal variation of the driving rough path vector field can be arbitrary p > 1, and to handle equations with two distinct transport mechanisms (a rough path-driven term and a DiPerna–Lions-type drift term).
AI.method: Constructs a higher-order unbounded rough driver framework grounded in rough paths over vector fields, allowing an Eulerian perspective. This framework accommodates driving rough paths with temporal p-variation for all p ∈ (1,∞), and is applied to establish well-posedness for a two-term transport equation.

title: The weak-type (1,1) bound for the Hardy--Littlewood maximal function is $O(\sqrt{n} \log n)$
summary: We prove a weak-type $(1,1)$ estimate for the centered Hardy--Littlewood maximal function with respect to Euclidean balls with dimensional dependence $O(\sqrt{n} \log n)$. This improves the order of growth in the classical $O(n)$ estimate of Stein and Strömberg. The proof goes through a pointwise bound of the Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator by the heat maximal operator with $\sqrt{n}$ loss. The key technical aspect of our result is an improvement of the weak-type bound for the heat maximal operator from $O(\sqrt{n})$ to $O(\log n)$.

AI.method: The proof uses a pointwise bound of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator by the heat maximal operator with only a √n loss, combined with an improved weak-type bound for the heat maximal operator from O(√n) down to O(log n).
AI.result: A weak-type (1,1) estimate with dimensional dependence O(√n log n) is established, improving upon the classical O(n) bound.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is reducing the dimensional growth from linear to roughly √n·log n, achieved through a key technical improvement of the heat maximal operator's weak-type bound to logarithmic order.
